speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I may be allowed, I would say that I have no objec-

War Appropriation-National Health
tion to blackout precautions or to the A.R.P., and I never had any. My contention is that they should be instituted only if necessary in central Canada. To show my position in the matter, let me say that I was the first person who raised in this house-in September 1939-the question of a home guard and the protection of provincial and municipal property on the same lines as in the last war. I find that the minister has been very fair in this matter. I call attention to the fact that away back in 1938 I raised this very subject during the discussion of the minister's estimates, on March 24. I then said, in part:
More consideration should be given to air defences. There is not only the possibility but a great probability that air raids will occur in the next war in which Canada is involved. The defence of our population from air raids should be considered. These raids will be the chief source of danger in all future wars, and we shall be living in a false paradise if we do not adopt measures to protect ourselves. Abyssinia was recently a theatre of war, and we all know the destruction of civilian population that occurred through this means of attack. Abyssinia is an open country with only a small density of population as compared with what there is on the island of Montreal and in other parts of Canada, and yet great damage resulted.
Air raids can work great havoc in time of war, and the menace will be a very real one in Canada, especially to the people of Quebec, the maritimes and British Columbia. I am glad that some preparation, although it may be only a beginning, has already been made by the minister to meet this danger. I know he has been out looking over the camps. A fleet of aircraft could pass up the Ottawa river without a moment's notice and blow up these buildings, the Chateau Laurier, the railway station and other large buildings. We should have very little warning of the approaching attack.
I was urging the establishment of a home guard.
Consultation and advice are words that are much used by the government nowadays, but we would not be consulted about any air raids that were contemplated against Canada. The enemy's aircraft would be upon us before you could say "O Canada," or sing God Save the King. An aerial bombardment is one of the dangers most to be apprehended in time of war, particularly in large cities with their dense populations; the protection of cities from aerial bombardment should be one of the chief objectives of the national defence department and proper equipment for defence against this menace should be provided. Probably the minister will have something to say about that later on.
Large quantities of poisonous gas could easily be spread over a large area as was done in Abyssinia, and incendiary bombs dropped on our large cities, with great destruction and slaughter, and the enemy aircraft could get back to their base in practically no time. These attacks would not only bring ruin to our cities and towns but break the morale of our people and prevent us from developing a proper defence and mobilizing our man-power and armaments.
In conclusion, I have never made any criticism of A.R.P. I referred last evening and last session nine or ten times to the good work they are doing. I did urge, however, that in central Canada the one hour blackout is too long. The British government has removed most of these restrictions, as Right Hon. Mr. Morrison, Home Secretary, said. In the Toronto district however one hour blackouts are enforced very strictly, and as we know, one of our own ministers was fined here for smoking his pipe. Yet, as has been pointed out by the Toronto papers at the time, a year ago:
Over in London, where they are a lot closer to nazi bombs and airmen than we are, and where they know a lot about blackouts, people are not forbidden to smoke pipes, or even cigarettes, in the streets. Actually, there are lights-green and red light crosses-at all the intersections of London streets, and most people go about with pencil flashlights. More than that, on Britain's country roads people drive about at night with suppressed or limited headlights on their motor cars.
I have not objected on any occasion to my friends the A.R.P. people. The statement I made was clear and I think it was quite fair. As I said, there is no such thing as home defence, as was proved when the mechanized hordes of Germany invaded the low countries. I do object to some of the newspaper reports. I refer to references in two or three papers in the Montreal district, regarding my stand on this and other questions. I ask the minister if I have on any occasion objected to the A.R.P. people. I have been a warm supporter of home defence and the good A.R.P. work and the minister's policy.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health): I am very glad to agree with my hon. friend. I have received from him complete cooperation at all times, although he thinks that blackouts have been carried out too extensively over the whole area; apart from that I have had complete cooperation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Was this item passed last night?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, it. was carried last night.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It is not so shown in Hansard; I have just looked it up.
May I say that I have always thought that A.R.P. was a good precautionary measure in the early stages of the war, but I do suggest that the thing might very well taper off now, when the danger of invasion has passed. As long as there was danger of



War Appropriation-National Health
invasion our people were quite justified in going as far as they did, and I would not like to see our precautions relaxed on the Pacific coast. I do not speak with any authority, but my partner happens to be the head of the A.R.P. organization in my constituency; I know the interest he takes in the matter, and he now thinks it ought to be washed out, and I hope it will be.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: My hon. friend was not here last night when I made reference to the very happy change in conditions in Canada. He will recall as well as I do that I was severely criticized a year and a half or two years ago, and there was an eloquent appeal from the leader of the opposition that the government form a ministry of home security.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I meant every word of it, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am not critical of that; I thought it was a constructive suggestion, but I am pointing out the change in conditions in the dominion and the change in the thinking of our people. At the same time, the responsibility is mine and we cannot afford to relax our efforts. I do not think we should expand any more. As I pointed out last night, as regards equipment, this year's estimates provide for practically all that we shall require, and the estimates will go down from now on for A.R.P. work. There is no intention of expanding, but, I repeat, it is my responsibility to support the volunteers, especially on the two coasts, in Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, British Columbia and parts of Ontario, in the splendid voluntary efforts they are making on behalf of the nation. We cannot afford to be extravagant, but on the other hand we cannot afford to be complacent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am fairly close in my own part of Canada to A.R.P. work. In parts of my own constituency there is an excellent organization. There has been, from the early part of the war until now, a sort of esprit de corps among the civilians flowing from A.R.P. precautionary measures, and I am inclined to think that whatever else they may have contributed, and I am not by any means limiting their contribution to this, they did provide an outlet for patriotic and serious-minded Canadians to make some physical move such as is manifested in the work they are doing in this field, which was particularly within their scope. Many of these men were of course veterans of the last war. A good many of the leaders in A.R.P. work throughout Canada are returned soldiers. It was a normal and a natural thing therefore for these men,

when this war broke out, to wish to get into work of some kind, into the army if possible but having been denied that on physical grounds they sought some other means of helping their country, as they had done in previous years.
The A.R.P. work has developed to the point where, in my opinion, Canadians may properly take a good deal of pride in the organization. I realize that one of the great troubles with the minister, and the late head of air raid precautions, was the fact that when the reserve army had been brought to the point where public recognition was given it in any major degree, and where the public, by various public relations measures and by appeals, had contributed to the enhanced importance of the reserve army in the estimation of the Canadian people, especially when the men were given uniforms and were thus more closely approximating actual war activities, the A.R.P. organization felt the drain very heavily upon their ranks, when men began to move into the reserve army. That naturally made it more difficult to keep the A.R.P. organization alive. But there was another factor which entered into the picture, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury has pointed out, namely, the growing conviction in the public mind of the danger of air raids to Canada. That was another factor which must have made it still more difficult for the head of the A.R.P. organization to keep it functioning.
We may properly pay tribute to Doctor Manion and his organization in connection with A.R.P. work. I mentioned before, and I refer to it again, the indomitable enthusiasm of Doctor Manion. Whatever may be said about the late lamented Doctor Manion, one fact that does stand out, in addition to the many other qualifications he had, was that when he undertook a job he threw every bit of energy and effort into it, and, what is more important, he devoted to it all the enthusiasm he possessed. I remember when he was first appointed how satisfied the minister was because he had been able to induce Doctor Manion to take on the work. I can remember too the time, two or three sessions ago, when I must confess I shared the view that was held by a good many people, and I am not so sure that it was not also the minister's view. At any rate, he kept his head cool while the debate was going on, but I must admit that I felt at that time that Canada was in a very dangerous position in regard to air raids. There was plenty of evidence from time to time to show that from various parts of the western coast of Europe German bombers could come over with their loads of destruction and return. That caused a great deal of fear in

War Appropriation-National Health
the minds and hearts of Canadians generally, and I for one felt-as I say, I am not so sure that the minister did not also feel-that some real move should be made to safeguard our people in the event of some untoward action, so that they might be adequately protected as far as humanly possible. Having in mind the steps that were then taken, and the renewed1 effort that was made in connection with A.R.P. work and its development to the point where Doctor Manion left it, I do not think that we should relax our efforts at this time. When we are nearing the end of hostilities we may be able to form a different judgment, but particularly in my own part of the country, which is the only part I can speak of with any degree of accuracy or of actual knowledge, I do not think it would be regarded as a wise move on the part of the government to relax the efforts that are now being made. I say this not only for security reasons but because A.R.P. work has proved an outlet for the activities of those of our citizens who wish to contribute to the war effort.
May I point out that we are not by any means out of the woods. It is quite true that we have reached the end of the beginning and are now at the beginning of the end, but we may find this period through which we are now passing a grave one for our people, however optimistic we may feel. We may have to go through several periods of great difficulty so far as the war in general is concerned. It may be that we shall have set-backs which to-day we cannot envisage. In the days that lie ahead we may find that this continent must suffer air attack, because before. Germany is beaten to her knees she will take many long chances and many retaliatory measures, one of which may be the bombing of defenceless people on this continent. If that is the case, and I am only throwing that out as a possibility, then I suggest to the government that we should not relax until we have seen the war move closer to a successful conclusion. Until that time I believe we should continue all these precautions which are necessary for the security of the average individual in this country who is doing his best on the home front.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It is not my desire to hold up the estimates of the minister, but I should like to add my word of praise of that great band of workers who have done so nobly in connection with A.R.P. work. It is not generally recognized, nor do I think it has been mentioned during this debate, that if a raid should take place the A.R.P. workers will be the first line of defence. Some people seem to thi*k that our home defence army will be 72537-3061
called into action first, but in the event of a raid the A.R.P. will be in the front line of battle, for they will be called into action immediately the raid takes place.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury pointed out that the government might relax its efforts in some districts. If that should be done I suggest to the minister that he should strengthen the organization in other districts, because to my mind the danger on the Pacific coast is not yet gone. I speak as a layman, but sometimes a layman may have a better understanding of the situation than some of our generals. I remember very well that when General Stuart went to the Pacific coast about two years ago and was told about the Japanese on Kiska, he laughed and said, "Oh, that little thing; that does not mean anything." Yet the other evening in his address to the House of Commons the Prime Minister stated that Kiska was a very important strategic point for the Japanese, and to-day no one can tell what may happen in the Pacific area. According to my information the strength of the Japanese remains intact; therefore I would suggest to the minister that if there are districts in which A.R.P. precautions may not be necessary, he take the money from those districts and spend it where we believe this organization should be strengthened. Those who are doing A.R.P. work have never received official recognition. Rifles and uniforms have been given to all other voluntary bodies, but the A.R.P. workers have had to put up a long fight in order to obtain the assistance they are being given to-day.
I just wanted to take this opportunity to expresss my thanks to that body of willing workers who are not officially recognized and who I think deserve such recognition.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
You will have plenty
of support in that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I wonder if the minister could enlighten the committee in regard to what A.R.P. work is being done in the smaller communities. The hon. member for New Westminster has mentioned the Pacific coast, where there are some large cities. When we think of bombings we usually associate them with cities such as Vancouver, Halifax and so on, but I believe there are many very important small communities that might become the objectives of the Japanese air force, let us say. I need make no secret about it; I do not suppose it is any secret that in Alberta, for instance, there is a chain of air training schools running from the United States boundary all the way up to Edmonton and perhaps beyond that point. These schools are closer to Kiska island than either Vancouver or Victoria. These air training schools are not
4834	COMMONS
War Appropriation-National Health
built out in the wilderness; they have very fine locations, and some are adjacent to small communities. Of course I do not know whether these schools would be regarded as military objectives; I do not know what value they would have as such. I know they do not constitute forts; they do not constitute munitions works, but they are highly specialized schools for the training of airmen, and there are many of them; make no mistake about that. Not very long ago I told one Liberal member here that I had six air training schools in my constituency. He was very much surprised, and wondered what I had done to get so many of these establishments located in my territory. I did not do a thing about it, but I believe the authorities used good judgment in putting them there. That is just my constituency; there are many other schools right along the mountains, where facilities for air training are good. If those air training schools should become the objectives of the Japanese air force, certainly the small communities near by would get it also. So far as I know the only thing that has been done is to train the people of those communities to put out their lights during blackouts. I do not know whether it is a very difficult undertaking to train people to turn out their lights, but in any case I should like to know whether anything more has been done.
While I am on my feet I should like to ask the minister for further information on another matter. This may not come under his department, but I am sure his knowledge extends beyond his own department. Are facilities available for giving plenty of warning in case a raid is made? I have in mind that a fleet of bombers, starting from somewhere off the Pacific coast, could follow a route clean across southeastern Alberta. Those bombers can fly several hundred miles an hour, as we know; they could cover a thousand miles in a very short time. How are these small communities to be warned in time to give adequate protection? I should like the minister to tell us what facilities have been established in that regard. I have no doubt there is some organization looking after that matter, but there is a great danger of focusing our attention upon some large metropolis and forgetting these small but strategic places.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Referring to the first question, there are certain areas in Canada which have been designated by the chief of staffs committee as either subject to definite risk or lesser risk. Of course the two coasts would be subject to definite risk, and practically all the coastal 
areas are under the A.R.P. system. In regard to the other areas, in British Columbia alone there are 139 local centres where they have air raid precaution organizations. In Canada altogether there are 633 areas.
In regard to the second point raised by the hon. member, having to do with training camps, may I say that the air force authorities have organizations of their own which are trained along similar lines to the air raid precautions organization, and they look after situations such as have been described by the hon. member. That area as such, however, does not come within the definition of a designated area, under the jurisdiction of this department, or the air raid precautions system.
As to the further point raised by the hon. member, may I point out that the air raid detection corps in Canada works in absolute liaison with the air raid precautions authorities. I know that in British Columbia, after some experiments, we found we were able to have the whole area blacked out inside of three minutes, through the use of most excellent telephonic communications. I believe, roughly speaking, I have replied to the points raised by the hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to make one or two references to this item. Before doing so however may I say that in my opinion the work being done by air raid precautions wardens is of so commendable a nature that it has earned the gratitude and approval of all hon. members. Recently I had the opportunity of seeing what is being done in Ottawa. I visited an exhibition given one Sunday in connection with fire-fighting, and at that [DOT] time I saw some of the work these men are doing. There is no glamour in the work they do. But they give hours of patriotic service, with no incentive other than the desire to contribute something at this time so that they may prepare themselves to protect us, should conditions make necessary the use of their knowledge. Nothing destroys discipline in any organization so much as the work of that organization becoming merely routine. In those circumstances enthusiasm may be lost, and all they have left to impel them to continue their efforts is their own appreciation of what they are doing. I do feel that there should not be any '[DOT]elaxation in the efforts of these men, many of whom were soldiers in the last war, and who in this way find an opportunity of doing something which otherwise would be denied them, namely the opportunity of serving in the only capacity for which they are fitted.
While at the present time we are in a period of what might almost be described

War Appropriation-National Health
as apathy in Canada so far as the danger of air raids is concerned, I cannot help recalling that only three months before Pearl Harbor a former member of Japan's intelligence service informed the members of the united nations that there would be a Pearl Harbor. He warned, too, that the Aleutians would be occupied. The hon. member for New Westminster has pointed out the strategic importance of the occupation of those islands. In addition to that he warned it was part of Japan's plan to bomb Pacific coast cities, down into the United States.
As the leader of the opposition has said, when the war approaches a crisis and the axis nations begin to appreciate that the sound of doom is about them, they may commence air raids merely because of their nuisance value. They may distribute gas in this way, and at such time, if it ever comes, the efforts of these men will be appreciated by the people of Canada. If we were to relax in this work or give it up we would invite the very thing the air raid precautions organization was intended to prevent.
May I ask the minister whether or not the various munitions plants in Canada, or any of them, have been warned about the dangers of air raids, and the necessity of making an appeal for volunteer blood donors?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Both things have been done. They have been warned in regard to both points mentioned by the hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: As to the hon. member's first question, I understand there is a security division in all munitions plants operated under the Department of Munitions and Supply. The main function of such divisions is exactly that mentioned by the hon. member. May I inform the hon. member that we have produced, to date, approximately 100,000 bottles of blood serum, part of which has been distributed to strategic centres in Canada, and all of which is available for any eventuality.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: For overseas.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Part of it has gone overseas. There have been received from the Connaught laboratories 79,174 bottles or cans of dried serum, 1,561 bottles or 223 boxes each containing seven bottles of serum, an equal number of distilled water and four giving sets have been dispatched overseas to date. Supplies are now in hand to dispatch similar boxes at the rate of 1,000 units of dried serum per week. There have been distributed in Canada and Newfoundland at strategic points for the armed services and civilian use when necessary through national catastrophes or enemy action, 39,131 bottles. The exact distribution is not disclosed because of the need of security. Competent authorities in every district and command, including A.R.P. and Red Cross, have knowledge as to their availability. There have been transported overseas 40,043 bottles.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Having in mind what
has been said in the committee this morning and which represents, I believe, the general view throughout the country, as to the necessity of keeping our air raid precautions intact in view of a possible dangerous situation arising a little later, I suggest that it would be advisable for the government not to postpone any longer the appointment of a successor to the late Doctor Manion, who was acting as director of air raid precautions. I aim afraid that if this appointment is delayed for any considerable length of time, those

War Appropriation-National Health
who are connected with this work may take it as evidence that the government has in mind the disbanding of the whole organization. That is not the proper attitude to take. If the government is desirous of keeping up the esprit de corps of this organization it should appoint as quickly as possible some outstanding Canadian citizen, as it did in making the previous appointment.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I made a recommendation to council a week ago, but because of other duties I was not able to be in council for the last two days. I may say that council has approved the appointment of General Alexander Ross, of Saskatchewan, formerly president of the Canadian Legion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I rise at this time on behalf of the people in my constituency to pay a tribute to the former director of A.R.P. We were heartsick when we heard of the sudden call of Doctor Manion to his "well done, good and faithful servant." That was his last task, and with all his brilliance he carried it out most efficiently. I do not think any public man from the head of the lakes has received a greater tribute from the public generally and from the press than did Doctor Manion. I was sorry I was not in the chamber before, but I take this opportunity of paying my tribute to him because he was one who was worthy to be trusted, and he was one who merited commendation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I agree with the
minister that this A.R.P. work should not be disbanded. We should not have any feeling of complacency about it. Things change quickly these days; new methods come along, and we do not know from day to day what is going to happen. As the minister remembers, during the early stages of the war I was most insistent upon something being done in connection with A.R.P. The people of Toronto were upset because of the number of factories in their immediate vicinity and their proximity to Niagara Falls. We cannot say that all danger of bombing has disappeared so far as our city is concerned; it is still within the bounds of possibility that something of the kind may happen.
I should like to pay a tribute to the men and women of Toronto who have given of their time to this work, and also to the members of the police force. The inspectors of the different divisions have given lectures which were most helpful, and generally an esprit de corps has been built up which is a credit to the citizens of that city. These people have attended lectures after doing * 
their day's work to learn about gases, first aid, fire fighting and so on. We should consider this expenditure as an insurance premium and hope that we will never have to make a claim. In order that this esprit de corps may not be lost, in order that these A.R.P. wardens may retain their enthusiasm, something should be done toward directing their efforts in some other direction. They could be used in some other form of useful war effort, especially in those places which are not in such great danger. I do not want it to be thought that the policemen and the firemen of Toronto are tired of this work; they have been most enthusiastic about it, and I think they welcomed an opportunity to participate in A.R.P. work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The turn the discussion on this item of $6,589,650 for air raid precautions has taken is disquieting to me. Some hon. members have contended that we should cut down on our expenditures and relax our A.R.P. work. That is a most dangerous outlook, one which I wish to repudiate at once. Many hon. members have adopted an apologetic attitude toward this work; they do not seem to understand why it is still necessary. My home is on the Pacific coast, and in that regard the minister and I are in the same position. When I wake up in the morning frequently one of the first things I think of is whether my home city has been bombed. That is no idle fancy. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) referred to the statement made by the Prime Minister on July 9, and I quote his words as reported on page 4558 of Hansard:
Kiska remains a potential centre of attack upon our shores, and upon other parts of this continent.
Larger planes are being built, and planes that can fly greater distances, and it has been admitted that it would be comparatively easy for an aeroplane carrier to slip up to within bombing range of the Pacific coast. It might not get away again, but the planes from such a ship could do great damage. I urge upon the minister that he pay no attention to these doubting Thomases. I urge him not only to carry on the air raid precautions work that has been initiated, but to go much farther. For example, I believe it is only within the last few days that the air raid wardens on our coast have received uniforms, and I understand that only a small number of them have been fitted out with these.
Some complaint has been made about blackouts being too long. For goodness' sake let us put up with a little inconvenience in order to make dead sure that we can have an efficient

War Appropriation-National Health
blackout when the need arises. The organization of air raid precautions is not yet perfect; it is far from perfect, and I think the minister would be the first to admit it. From the start, it has been difficult to organize because there has been divided authority between the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities. It has been a great stuggle to get this work going at all, and I do urge upon the minister that further efforts be made to improve the general organization.
The government is to be congratulated on appointing General Alex. Ross as director of air raid precautions for Canada. I had what I consider one of the greatest privileges of my life in being able to serve under General Ross in France during the year 1918. He is an outstanding leader of men, probably one of the finest leaders of men that Canada has produced in our generation. That at least is my personal opinion. I believe in General Ross- Turkey Ross, as he was known to the troops-
I believe in him right through the picture. He is no yes-man-the minister knows that, the men of the Canadian Legion know that. He will make demands on the government and he will be pretty tough about those demands. He will want to get proper backing, and I urge upon the minister that he stand behind General Ross in this work. The minister has already had an excellent director in the late Doctor Manion; he could have had no better man. May I urge upon him that he stand behind Doctor Manion's successor, and if he does we may take it for granted that the air raid precautions work in Canada will be carried on in an efficient manner.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I wish to associate myself with the tribute which has been paid by the leader of the Progressive Conservative party to the work done by Doctor Manion and by the wardens and others who have assisted in carrying out the air raid precautions work throughout Canada. Amongst them were members of the St. John Ambulance Brigade, who have been very active in even- part of Canada and have done excellent work.
May I say a few words in support of the statements made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) yesterday, when he called attention to some dangers and difficulties in connection with the blackouts. While I would not for a moment wish to disagree with the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) in regard to the necessity for blackouts on the Pacific coast, and also the Atlantic coast and in Quebec province, yet I think that the blackouts in the interior of Canada might very well be shortened in duration; for instance, in the big cities like Toronto,
Kingston, not forgetting Ottawa, and perhaps Montreal. But that is a matter for the department, and having said a word in regard to it I am quite willing to leave it to the judgment of those in authority.
I have asked a few questions about A.R.P. work which have not yet been answered, but I presume I may expect an answer shortly from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I have a memorandum here, but I have not yet analysed it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Then I will not ask for it at
this time; it can be supplied later.
I am satisfied with the statement made earlier this morning by the minister when he said that this work would be continued in the maritimes, in Quebec and on the Pacific coast just as actively as it had been done heretofore, but less so in the central provinces where less expenditure may be made. It was this question of the reduction in cost to which I wished to call attention in one of the questions which I asked in regard to this work.
I want to commend the minister himself for the work he and his department have done in initiating and carrying through the work of A.R.P.
I would like while on my feet to refer-if it is necessary I will do it on a question of privilege-to what was said by the hon. member for Brantford City last night in my absence from the house. He apparently got the view that I was making a personal attack on the minister. I want to disavow any such intention, and if my words created any such impression I am very sorry. I only wished to bring to the minister's attention as forcefully as I could the reasons why I, in common with a large body of opinion in Toronto and elsewhere, was opposed to his going ahead with additions to Christie Street hospital. Perhaps he had reference to the words I used in regard to a monument in Toronto. If so, I would say to the minister that he can very well change the character of that monument if he will do as we suggest, put up a new building, and I am quite willing then to propose that it be called the Mackenzie Military hospital.
Only one word further in regard to the argument of the hon. member for Brantford City in support of his opinion that noises would not interfere with the use of a stethoscope. I think possibly the word of a consulting physician who complained to me would be taken as of more value than that of the hon. member for Brantford City.
Item agreed to.

War Appropriation-National Health
Health branch-Industrial hygiene, including inspection of industrial plants, $24,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I hope we are on the right item now. This item was read out before and I rose to speak but I was interrupted. I said when I spoke before that I think the amount of 824,000 is entirely too small for this purpose and that it should be at least ten times that much. The reason I say that is that the health of the workers in our plants is not really looked after as it should be. That is why we have so much absenteeism. Many of the young boys and young girls who go into these plants have not had their fathers or mothers teach or show them the proper methods of keeping in good health. Therefore it is up to this government to do it. An article in a Kitchener newspaper of July 14 says that ten cases of active tuberculosis have been discovered in the plants there. A complete survey has been made of over seven thousand workers, among whom ten active cases of tuberculosis were discovered. These ten active cases can be checked if taken in hand now, and these people can be built up into first-class shape. This survey was made by a Doctor Fraser-he is no relation of mine-who is evidently the medical health officer of Kitchener. But in most cities the medical health officer is so busy that he has not a chance to do this work. I spoke of this matter in the house last year and I am bringing it up again because I do feel that the government should maintain a proper supervision over all the workers in these plants. The Department of Agriculture have a check-up on the live stock in Canada, but our human beings are neglected. If these people were checked we would have a better Canada after this war is over; and if we ever intend to have social security we should start in now to improve the health of these people.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to add a word to what has been said by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I too feel that the appropriation for this particular phase of the department's work is insufficient and inadequate. After all, the Department of Pensions and National Health is interested in labour conditions as well as in health conditions, because the conditions under which workers work may lead to good health or bad health as the case may be. For example, back in January I was in a plant which makes acids and gases and so on, and I asked the manager of this very large plant, because I was there at noon and saw the men sitting around eating their lunch on any packing case or barrel which happened to be in the furnace

rooms, whether there was any provision for a cafeteria or restaurant where they might take their lunch under conditions which would be eleanly and healthful, and the answer was no.
I am not complaining about our government plants. I must say that a few days ago I was in our small arms ammunition factory near Quebec city, and there I saw a splendid cafeteria, rest rooms and lavatory accommodation and excellent food provided in this government plant, and I was deeply impressed by the care that had been taken to look after the health of the workers there. But in some of the other plants-and I have no hesitation in mentioning names; I was in the Canadian Carbide plant at Shawinigan Falls-there was no such accommodation where men could eat at noon under cleanly conditions. Of course the Department of Labour is interested in the matter, but this is a department of health, I think the appropriation is insufficient for the kind of work which the department needs to undertake, and I miss my guess if the minister, who is giving a tremendous amount of attention to this sort of thing, does not agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I thank both hon. members for their observations. I might point out at once that we are not limited to this amount-this is a war appropriation-and if the department finds it necessary to increase the amount beyond $24,000 I do not think we would have much difficulty in obtaining the necessary money.
I am informed that we have already inspected about 300 plants for such purposes; and from a nutrition point of view we have inspected 500 industries. That is not under this vote, but the nutrition aspect is also being given attention. Eighteen of these plants had no medical or safety services of any kind, and in over fifty others the first aid services were very inadequate, with no provision for medical care or safety control. All these things have been corrected. We started this work in 1942. I can say that the most rigid attention is paid in all the plants over which the government has control to carrying out the regulations and the provisions of the Geneva code.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: May I say that in Kitchener 8,700 workers were X-rayed for tuberculosis. It is important now to check for tuberculosis, especially at this time when meat and other foods are rationed.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Is not the X-ray work done by the provincial government?

War Appropriation-National Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It may be done by the provincial government, but this government should ensure that it is done. People are not getting the nourishment which they were getting before the war, and that is why there is a greater risk of tuberculosis among our young people. With regard to one plant which I know of, and I suppose the same conditions obtain all over the country, they have nurses to look after their workers; in the rooms where the nurses are they will have large jars of aspirin tablets, and if a girl comes in and says she has a headache the nurse will say, " Help yourself." Many of these young girls will take one, three, four, five or ten aspirin tablets, not knowing what is wrong with them. If there were a doctor or someone qualified to check the condition of that girl she could be fixed up right away. I know of two girls who were seriously unwell because, not having been examined, they took aspirins until they got in such a weakened condition that it required months for their recovery.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am glad to get that information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There are a number of things in connection with the minister's department on which I can very frankly and sincerely congratulate him. One of them is the health services which he has initiated in these factories. I am thinking particularly of the plant at Malton and the improvement which has been made in the facilities for safeguarding the health of the workers since it came under direct government ownership and supervision. The set-up there is the finest I have seen in any plant which I have visited.
I have noticed that there is a considerable degree of difference in the facilities available as between one plant and another, and I would just like to remind the minister, although I do not think it necessary, that the collection of large numbers of men in war industries is giving his department an opportunity for improving or for taking the first steps in the improvement of the health of the nation-an opportunity which probably will not be available in peace time. We now have plants which are directly under government supervision and working on government orders. Large numbers of men are congregated in these centres. I urge upon the minister that he take advantage of that opportunity to give the nation a start on the road to better health. I need not emphasize the fact that the war has shown that we have been very neglectful of that in the past.
There are one or two other topics upon which I should like to occupy a minute, Mr. Chairman, if you will be gracious enough to permit me. I wish to second1 the suggestion made by the hon. member for Parkdale. I was astonished that a Progressive Conservative representing a Toronto riding would suggest that Toronto would be willing to call a military hospital the Ian Mackenzie military hospital.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Only on certain conditions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I presume it is because they have a personal attachment to the minister, rather than to the government which he represents.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It is because they want the hospital.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It almost persuades me that the Conservatives are becoming progressive.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: They have been, right along.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
However, I hope the minister will take it into consideration. I did not have an opportunity to speak when the subject was under review, but everyone who knows anything about the situation in Toronto 

those in charge of the war veterans' associations, the doctors, and various welfare organizations-has made representations. The minister is familiar with these representations, and I am sure we need' not take time to try to impress him with the need of remedying that situation. I think the remedy suggested, the necessity of finding a new site as soon as possible to begin the erection of a new hospital, is the solution. I thank you Mr. Chairman, for permitting me to make this remark on this item.

Item agreed to.
Health branch-Laboratory analyses and ser-vxces for the Department of National Defence, $37,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There are a few questions which I wish to ask with reference to this item. I have already pointed out that, in my opinion and in the opinion of many other people as well, the Canadian people are not getting the nutrition they were before the war, and the reason for this is rationing. Reports from Montreal indicate a rising death rate from tuberculosis. I was wondering what the government would do withvregard to vitamin B in Canada-approved 'flour. This is a matter

War Appropriation-National Health
which concerns the department, and I submit that something should be done. I have here a series of questions which I should like to submit to the minister:
1.	In view of the unsatisfactory results attained by the government's programme to introduce a vitamin B white flour made exclusively by the so-called "long extraction" milling process, as evidenced by the testimony submitted at the conference held in Ottawa, January 5 and 6 last, does the government now purpose to modify the restrictions against synthetic enrichment of flour with such vitamins as are deemed deficient, by your nutritional advisers, in the national dietary; particularly under war conditions?
2.	Since approximately fifty per cent of the flour used in Canada is baked by the housewife and the larger proportion of it in the form of bread, and since she has become accustomed to using the so-called "top patent" or "family" grade as being most satisfactory for the purpose, and since this grade carries the lowest natural vitamin content of any of the hard wheat flours milled, namely 50 to 100 I.U's per pound, how is it proposed to increase the vitamin intake of the Canadian people unless this grade of flour is improved by synthetic addition?
3.	In Ontario and generally in eastern
Canada most cakes, biscuits, pastries are made from soft winter wheat flour, both commercially and home baked.	Ontario
winter wheat is much lower in vitamin value than hard spring (bread) wheat flour. How can the vitamin intake from this source be increased except by the use of synthetics?
4.	Since it has been established by the testimony at the January session above referred to that spring wheat flours of the 1942 crop will average 100 units or more per pound lower than the previous crop in natural vitamin B-l content, and since even from the 1941 crop wheat many mills had great difficulty in attempting to meet the 400 international units per pound requirement in the flour, and also since, to a great many bakers, this flour was entirely unsatisfactory in its baking qualities, how can it be hoped to produce a satisfactory flour with the -50 to -55 ash from the new (1942) crop wheat, at even the modest level of 400 I.U's per pound, unless synthetic enrichment is resorted to?
5.	In view of the established success of synthetic enrichment-of-fiour programme in the United States and the requirement of the cereal import committee in Great Britain that all Canadian flour shipped to that country shall be synthetically enriched with

vitamin B-l, why have we in Canada held back from adopting this scientifically improved means of increasing the vitamin intake in the national dietary with respect to breadstuffs?
Some people say that vitamins have a tendency to produce certain weaknesses, but that has never been proved. In the foregoing questions the word "synthetic" is not quite appropriate because the vitamins that are added to the flour are natural vitamins. If you added the so-called synthetic vitamin B to flour and baked a loaf of bread with it, and used the wheat berry to increase the vitamin B content in another batch of flour, baking a loaf of bread from that flour, I do not believe there is a man in the country who could tell the difference. I do not think there is anyone who could say which was the synthetic product and which was the bread made from the natural wheat berry, because if both samples were subjected to the fluorescent lights which are used for testing they would fluoresce in the same way. I should like the minister to tell us what is being done, because the people should have these extra vitamins and they will not buy bread unless it is white, though when it is made in the ordinary way the vitamins are killed.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
My hon. friend has raised a highly technical question which I doubt that I am competent to discuss in technical terms. A year and a half or two years ago we had a committee of the greatest nutritional experts in Canada, including the dominion cerealist and experts from our own department, and they agreed, after consultation and various experiments, scientific and otherwise, upon this standard of Canada-approved flour. It has been very well received though there was some resistance from some of the millers. I know, from information given me by experts from other countries, that it is the opinion of the highest nutritional experts in Great Britain that our Canada-approved flour, which comes from the natural wheat, has a finer nutritive value than any synthetically induced proportions of vitamin that go into any other flour. Britain herself to-day is not using synthetic flour to the extent that she was; she is exporting quite a bit to other countries. It is the opinion of experts in the United States and Britain that our high extraction flour is superior for the health of the nation, and I should not be surprised to see them reverting to our standard of flour before this argument is over. There is some resistance from certain millers at the present time, but I must rely upon the best scientific and technical advice I receive, not only from the officers of my own department but from those of

War Appropriation-National Health
other departments and from many eminent experts outside. The standard represents a great advance forward from what we had before, and there are certain definite constituents, such as iron, phosphorus and calcium, which are all of great benefit to the health of the individual and consequently to the health of the nation as a whole. I personally know little about the subject but the best advice I have received is as I have indicated.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: But you get those same constituents, iron, calcium and phosphorus, in the synthetic product, which is bakers' yeast.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: My information is to the contrary. Of course, I am only speaking from information I have received. The note I have on the point is that no evidence has been produced to show that these constituents, in the same percentage, are present in the yeast which was under consideration at that time.

Item agreed to.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.
Processing, storage and distribution of blood for transfusions, $120,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I presume this has to do with the processing and distribution of blood obtained through the blood donor clinics operated by the Red Cross. I should like to tell this committee of one of the finest examples of civilian cooperation in an international way that has come to my knowledge. Recently the good people of the city of Ogdensburg, New York, decided to open a blood donors' clinic and give their blood to the American Red Cross. It was found, however, that owing to the geographical location of that city, it was not practicable to send that blood to an American processing laboratory. The Ogdensburg chapter of the American Red Cross thereupon applied to the parent organization to see if it would be possible to send that blood to the Canadian Red Cross This permission was granted, and they applied to the Brockville branch of the Canadian Red Cross for assistance in setting up their clinic. Naturally that assistance was gladly given. The necessary formalities in regard to customs and immigration on both sides of the line have been settled, and the people of Ogdensburg are now in process of signing up nine hundred donors. They hope to have their clinic in
operation on or about August 1, at which time the blood will be collected by members of the Brockville branch, brought across the river and sent to Toronto for processing.
I think it is generally recognized that blood plasma is vitally needed at this time; and to me it is an inspiration to think that our American friends, when they found it impossible to give blood to their own organization, of their own free will should ask if they might present their blood to the Canadian Red Cross. As I say, I know of no finer example of international civilian cooperation, and I believe that we as Canadians could learn a lesson here. Even some hon. members of this house could learn a lesson from this incident. We have not enough blood donors in this country; I think anyone connected with the Department of Pensions and National Health will support that statement. We need more blood donors. I have already suggested that hon. members should go to the Ottawa branch of the Red Cross and donate their blood, and again I would urge them to do so. Surely if our American friends are willing to donate their blood to the cause of Canada and the cause of the united nations, we Canadians should intensify our efforts and have more people give their blood for the same cause.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I want to thank my hon. friend for his reference to what is really a magnificent gesture, for which we are profoundly grateful.

Item agreed to.
Grant to the Canadian Nurses' Association to increase the supply of qualified nurses in Canada, $250,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Will the minister give us a brief statement of what has been done in this connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Last year the grant was $115,000; this year it is being increased to $250,000. Last year the grant was made for the following purposes: $15,000 for administration expenses and to provide staff and travelling expenses, to stimulate the recruitment of student nurses and the expenses of publicity in connection therewith. Last year $75,000 was allocated to hospitals or other teaching institutions to provide additional facilities for the tuition of teachers, supervisors and administrators in schools of nursing, and for the training of the increased registration of student nurses. Then $25,000 was devoted to scholarships for graduate nurses for education as teachers, supervisors and administrators. As a result of the recruiting campaign the number of students in schools
4842	COMMONS
War Appropriation-National Health
of nursing was increased by 1,402. Some forty-five scholarships, ranging in value from $265 to $500, were awarded to approved candidates, eighteen for post-graduate work in nursing and twenty-one in public health.
The grant of $75,000 for teaching institutions was allocated through the provinces, to be used for the following purposes: refresher courses for graduate nurses, summer courses in public health nursing, teaching, supervision of hospitals and hospital administration; special clinical post-graduate courses for three months; field work for universities and schools of nursing; to assist smaller schools in providing additional staff, teaching equipment and text books to take care of the increased registration; to provide for smaller schools travelling specialized instructors in psychiatry, dietetics, pediatrics and communicable diseases.
The need for more graduate nurses and specialists has increased so that it is considered desirable to increase the assistance to the Canadian Nurses' Association as follows:
(a)	1 $25,000 for administration, to increase campaign for recruitment of student nurses, and for increased publicity.
(b)	$155,000 for direct assistance to schools of nursing to provide for increased registration. The present grant did not permit assistance to many schools where such aid would have provided for larger registration. It is planned to increase the number of students in many more training schools as soon as money can be provided for increased training facilities.
(c)	$40,000 for scholarships. The need for specialists is increasing. The grant last year permitted forty-five scholarships, but this took care of only half the eligible and desirable applicants.
(d)	' $30,000 for direct assistance to schools of nursing in universities and in public health organizations in order to extend their facilities for giving post-graduate specialist training. Present facilities are taxed to capacity and direct aid will provide for increased output of trained specialists. The method of distribution of the direct assistance to teaching institutions and universities is subject to the approval of the department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Has the minister any knowledge of the means that were employed by the nursing organization to encourage young ladies to enroll as pupil nurses? This seems like a good deal of money, and I was wondering if a canvass was made of the schools or anything like that, in order to encourage young ladies to become nurses.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, that was done by a field secretary employed by the nurses' association.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I believe this is another very important appropriation. I have had the opportunity in the last three years to know something of this training, and it seems to me if we are to make the nursing profession more attractive to the right type of girl, facilities will have to be provided so that more of them may be engaged in the work in unit hospitals, in order that they may not be overtaxed and their health may be protected. Not only here, but as a member of the hospital board in Regina, I have known that a large number of girls have broken their health during training. And when one considers that girls in training are not only doing hospital duties, but are also studying and preparing for examinations, it will be realized that their duties are those which only a girl in fairly robust health could possibly stand.
I am not complaining about the hospitals. But, as I say, I have had personal contact with one in the city in which I lived, and I have known something about the local situation. I do believe an attempt should be made by the government to encourage more young girls to come in so that they may relieve, at least to some extent, those who are already in training. This may mean that grants will have to be made for increased accommodation for student nurses attached to hospitals with approved training schools. Because, after all, in many such hospitals the number of student nurses who can be enrolled will be governed by the amount of accommodation the hospital has for student nurses in residence and in class rooms. I suggest this is something to which attention should be given by the government when it is making grants. The institutions themselves should be assisted to provide accommodation so that there will not be quite such long hours for some of the girls in the hospitals, and that more care-if I may put it in that way, although I know supervisors give all the attention they can-shall be given to the health of the girls in training. In a number of instances a very high percentage of student nurses have failed to complete the course, not only because some of them were unfit, but because of a breakdown in health, often the result of very strenuous work and the long hours.
I know that in most hospitals an attempt is made to limit the working day to eight hours. I also know, very well indeed, that it is almost impossible in some of these institutions to live up to that eight-hour regulation. The girls have to work nine and even ten hours sometimes. In addition they must study, which means that they cannot withstand the strain. In my opinion some con-

War Appropriation-National Health
sideration should be given to the provision of accommodation in training schools attached to our hospitals, sufficient to ensure that there will be an ample supply of student nurses in the future, and that none of the girls in training shall be overworked. I believe we should pay some attention to that aspect of the matter.
Mr, MACKENZIE (Vancouver Centre): We agree.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In his break-down the minister referred to scholarships for graduate nurses, so that they may take special training. Has any provision been made to assist student nurses who, because of the lack of a few dollars, might not be able to enroll for training purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I believe a definite statement was made on that subject by Miss Ellis before the social security committee, of which the hon. member is a member. My recollection is that there was no direct grant to student nurses. I am instructed they are expecting some assistance from one of the training schemes, but it had not been forthcoming before she gave her evidence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I was pleased to
hear the last report of the minister. My information is that the chief drawback to the securing of more nurses is, first, the fact that a great many girls cannot afford to take the three years, and, in addition to receiving no compensation for their work in the hospitals, be called upon to provide books and uniforms. Anything that could be done to relieve that situation would be helpful. I understand there are some hospitals in which a small remuneration is paid, but that condition is not general. That is the first big drawback. The second drawback is the number of hours these girls are asked to work. If the minister can do anything to relieve those two situations, he will go a long way toward achieving the end he has in view.
May I commend the minister on the amount of money he has set aside for this purpose. I certainly agree it is something that is very much needed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Are not
all arrangements with regard to pay and the terms of apprenticeship standardized? Are not the hours of labour in standard hospitals all the same? They were at one time.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am under the impression they are not. I think the objective has always been that they should be standardized at the level mentioned
by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. But I believe conditions do differ across Canada, even in our best hospitals.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I have
served on a hospital board for a number of years, and I thought it had always been recognized by the hospitals association that these things were standardized. However, I am glad to be informed on the point. If they are not, they ought to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am not speaking definitely, but I am under the impression that my statement is correct.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I think I can say definitely that all major hospitals have adopted the eight-hour day. For many years it was a twelve-hour day, but even at that I am happy to say that with the regular hours of sleep, the regular meals and the like, ninety-five per cent of the nurses put on flesh and gained in health during their course of training in the various hospitals. In those days there was a small monthly payment of $5, but I do not know whether or not that is paid to-day. But I believe I can allay the fears of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, because I have been connected in the west with a nursing school for a great many years, and I know that the vast majority of nurses who went into training gained in health in the first five or six months. And that was the condition in* the early days, when they spent twelve hours a day, and sometimes more, at their work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
While I realize that what
I am going to say is to some extent a provincial matter, yet I notice that the federal government is making a fairly substantial contribution to nursing, and there is one point I should bring to the minister's attention. One of the greatest causes of the shortage of nurses is that training privileges have been taken away from the small hospitals. Girls in the smaller towns cannot now train in most of the small hospitals, but are compelled to go to the larger cities. In many instances this is not looked upon with favour by their parents. I think the experience has been that many of our better nurses have been trained in some of the smaller hospitals throughout the country. I believe if the training privilege were restored to smaller hospitals we would not now have this shortage of nurses.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Is that not entirely a matter of provincial registration?

War Appropriation-National Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, I think it is.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I cannot quite agree with what was said by the hon. member for St. Boniface. My personal observation has been that while care is taken of the young nurses in training, yet owing to the pressure upon them, break-downs have developed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Veiy few.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I hesitate to mention anything that I might have observed during my own daughter's training which she has just completed, but in the class in which she trained there were, I believe, 54 pupils, and at the end there were some 38 left, the remainder being on the casualty list to some extent on account of break-down in health.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Probably some got married.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
None of them got
married, so far as I know, while they were in training. This does not seem to be much improvement over what I know was the case some years ago when I myself was on a hospital board. While I am not blaming the hospitals, because I know the pressure is tremendous, I do say that if we wish to get student nurses in our hospitals we shall have to see to it that the hours are not prolonged.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am not advocating
prolonged hours.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I understand that quite well; the hon. member advocated shortened hours. It frequently happens that the hours are unavoidably extended beyond eight because hospitals are under pressure and understaffed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: They overlap.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Some overlapping does occur. I do not want it to be thought that I feel that this matter does not need remedying, because, in my opinion it does.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
A wrong impression might be created in the minds of those who have occasion to review this particular debate. We must not get it into our heads that an eight hour day in an institution means eight hours of work for the nurses. That is to say, you could not possibly operate under three eight hour shifts and find work for the nurses to do. There must be quiet periods in a hospital, otherwise your patients will not get along as well as they should. This idea of talking about a twelve hour day or an eight hour day is all

wrong. I do not know of any institution that might be said to work on a twelve hour basis, where the nurses work a twelve hour day. They have their rest periods, particularly at night. The institution must be quiet. It is not a factory you are running; it is an institution for the healing of those [DOT]who come to your door. There is a great deal of confusion in the minds of people who feel they should run three eight hour shifts. You will be running a factory, not a hospital. I do not know of any place where they actually work, where they are on their feet for twelve hours. There is a rest period in the afternoon and a long rest period at night when the other work is off.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The busiest time for
hospital nurses is between ten o'clock at night and eight o'clock in the morning.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is this appropriation of a quarter of a million dollars for the training of nurses for the armed forces, or is it for the training of nurses for all the services? I realize that this is a war appropriation. To a large extent nurses, when they are available, are having to take the place of doctors because of the present shortage of doctors. I do not mean that they are doing all the work the doctors would do, because we know they do not. In Alberta they have certain health units which are made up of a number of communities. A doctor is the health officer for the entire territory. A number of doctors have joined the forces, others have moved away, and the result is that some of these health units are without doctors. The nurses have taken their places, not to do all that a doctor would do, but to substitute as much as possible. I hope that part of this money is to go for the training of nurses who will eventually find their way into civilian service. How is this money distributed? Is any of it given to the provincial governments to handle in connection with the training of nurses?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The moneys are distributed by nurses' associations and hospital associations with the approval of the director of public health services, Department of Pensions and National Health. This appropriation is for the training of nurses for all purposes, both military and civilian, so they would be available for the health units to which my hon. friend has referred. This necessity has been occasioned by the depletion in the ranks of the nurses caused by the war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to say a word in support of this grant. There is no body of professional people in the country more

War Appropriation-Justice
worthy of support than are our nurses. They are doing a magnificent job. The period during which they can work is limited and any assistance we can give toward the carrying out of their duties should be given. I do not know to what hospital the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) was referring, but might it not be possible that the examination made of the nurses before they went into training was not sufficiently thorough to determine whether they were in category A? In most hospitals an X-ray examination of the chest is made, and as a consequence this has practically eliminated the incidence of tuberculosis among nurses which used to be quite prevalent years ago. There is no standard of medical examination adopted by all hospitals; it depends upon the examiner in each hospital as to how rigidly the requirements of physical fitness are enforced before a student is admitted for training as a nurse. I thought possibly this might explain the casualty list amongst the student nurses to which my hon. friend referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: They did find a rather high incidence of tuberculosis among nurses in training, and that is why X-ray examinations are now made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am not complaining about the hospital to which I referred, because I believe it is probably one of the best in the country and is giving the best of training. My own daughter has completed her course without a break, but I happen to know that others have not been able to do so.

Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): There are only three items.
