These are the salaries and cost of living bonus of three
temporary employees who have been added to the sendee of the department. I did not think it necessary to have a memorandum prepared covering these small items, but I have one prepared for the larger item.

Mr. Chairman, I have for a very long while wished to have the opportunity to discuss democracy in this country. Now the opportunity has come, and I welcome it; for after the winning of the war there is no subject more important than the maintenance of democracy. On July 9 the Prime Minister, speaking in the house, said this:
Our conception of nationhood rejects, as it must always reject, any attachments to ideas which are non-democratic or to usages which would constitute the negation of free institutions or the untrammelled expression of the free souls of free men.
Those are very wonderful words. Mr. Chairman. I should like to see these things a living reality in this country. I must admit that resentment has been burning inside me for many months now because of the lack of an opportunity to discuss this very question, and I intend to use all the force of which I am capable to speak against the sort of administration we have had under these defence of Canada regulations.
I do not think I need emphasize the fact to any hon. member of this house that I was brought up in a country which is known as the mother of parliaments and the home of democracy. My freedom of speech and the right to associate as I please was something which was to me just like the air I breathe. It was my inalienable right. I am not unmindful either of all the things that were endured by my ancestors in days gone by and the price they had to pay for the freedom which they finally attained. I am not unaware of many who met their deaths in days gone by from the force and violence of those who sought to rob the common people of their freedom, and I should be untrue to those who have gone before and untrue to myself if at this time I failed to protest against a new form of despotism which is growing up within the boundaries of this country to dominate us and which like a cancerous growth impairs democracy. These may seem strong expressions to hon. members, but I can find no words too strong to express my feelings in this regard.
We do not miss the air we breathe until we gasp and choke for lack of it, and some people do not appreciate the rights and privileges they have until they have them snatched from them by force and violence. To see other little groups of people lose their privileges and rights does not affect us at all.
War Appropriation-Justice

It is only when we ourselves lie broken in spirit under the fetters of despotism that we realize its full calamity, and then, my friends, it is too late. While I have breath to protest against some things which have gone on in this country in the administration of the defence of Canada regulations I shall do it.
I should like to give one instance in which within the last few months the rights of one section of our people have been denied them, even though the Minister of Justice wields extraordinary power under these regulations. The question this time is that of freedom of speech. It is in connection with a meeting which should have been held in the city of Montreal on May 3 of this year. A large mass meeting had been arranged for in that city. Various trades union leaders were to speak and the leader of the communist party of Canada, who had spoken previously in every other large city across Canada, was also to be there. Although the hall had been engaged-I believe it was the Atwater market-at the last minute the meeting was cancelled. Nobody seemed to know why. The citizens who were interested in this meeting gathered themselves together for another meeting to protest. Peculiarly enough the second meeting was not allowed. Then this same group of citizens, swelling in numbers as the people gradually became aware of what had happened in their city, gathered together, and, roughly calling themselves "The Defenders of the Four Freedoms," arranged for a well known journalist in Montreal to prepare a broadcast on the question of freedom of speech for the people of that city. The journalist in question prepared a broadcast. It was accepted by the censor, and yet at the last moment he was not allowed to make that speech over the air. Finally, after some time, this group of people did get a conference together. I went down myself that evening. At that conference there were represented roughly 131 organizations in the city of Montreal, which would mean representing over 130,000 of Montreal's citizens. They met to protest the right of freedom of speech being denied to them as it had been accorded to the citizens of every other great city in this country. At the end of that conference they sent a letter to the Minister of Justice. They asked that they might have freedom of speech in their city the same as the people of any other city, well aware that no nation can live with its people half slave and half free. I have here a copy of the minister's reply to that group of people representing over 130,000 citizens. He says:
I have duly received your letter of June 4, with attached thereto copy of a resolution appealing to the Prime Minister of Canada to

instruct his Department of Justice that freedom of speech, press and assembly, such as is permitted to the rest of Canada, should also be accorded to the citizens of Quebec, and praying him, moreover, to employ the utmost latitude in assuring for all citizens of this dominion opportunity to exercise this fundamental right of a free people.
A similar letter has also been referred to me from the Prime Minister's office.
Then listen to this last paragraph:
I wish to inform you that the Department of Justice has nothing to do with the according of freedom of speech, press and assembly to the citizens of Quebec, any more than it has to do with such privilege in other provinces of Canada, and has not acted in any manner to which the criticism implied in this resolution would seem to be applicable.
In other words, although our Minister of Justice wields tremendous power, he claims that he has nothing to do with the privilege and right of freedom of speech in this country. I fail to understand why our Minister of Justice has not acted. Perhaps it would help the members of this house to understand one reason why the minister did not act when I say that finally it was known that a little group in Montreal were responsible for the stopping of this great public meeting. One of them particularly, a Mr. Raymond, a member of the other place, closely connected with the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie, and other groups in the province of Quebec has been most vocal against Canada's greatest and all-out participation in this war. They were the groups who were responsible for the stopping of these meetings in the city of Montreal. This is an astounding fact.
I would say that the minister's action, or rather his lack of action, to protect the democratic right of freedom of speech in that one city of Montreal, amounts to nothing more or less than appeasement of anti-war groups in the province of Quebec. After all, if there is one thing in this world worse than no justice, it is that there should be justice without a sword in her hand. We have witnessed the lights of Europe go out one by one. We have witnessed people lose their freedom little by little. We have seen the calamity which overtook those who viewed too carelessly this question of their democratic rights. It should be a lesson to us. We should resist these things in time. Whether or not we have any particular liking for the views of those who wish to speak is not the question. It matters not whether it be trades union leaders or the leader of the communist party who may be expressing views which may not be palatable to some. The fact remains that freedom of speech is the right of the people of this country at all times, pro-

War App rirpriation-Justice
vided that speech is towards a democratic end. It so happens that the speeches that were to be made were on behalf of the victory-loan. "Back the attack" was to have been the spirit of the meeting. Yet we find groups who have been most vocal against an all-out war effort by Canada being the ones to prevent this meeting in the city of Montreal.
I charge that under these defence of Canada regulations the Minister of Justice has not protected the rights of all the citizens of this country. Yet the purpose of his administration of these regulations is supposed to be that we should be protected from those who seek to destroy democracy within the boundaries of this country. It is pretty clear today all the world over that whoever denies the rights of the people is against the people, and whoever is against the people is their enemy. Let us not make any mistake about it.
So much then for the protection which should have been afforded to the people of Canada under the defence of Canada regulations. We accepted as a nation these regulations as a war emergency, designed only to protect us from the machinations of the enemy within our own country. But the minister has failed to use the authority which we have placed in his hands, to protect the citizens of Montreal. I will go further and say that while he has failed to protect us under these regulations, he has in some other ways used them to bar the progress of democracy in this country.
I would quote from the Toronto Telegram of June 24, which contains a dispatch that on June 23 Canada's Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in an address prepared for delivery to the Midwest Farm Bureau conference, said:	[DOT]
Reviewing war developments, Mr. Gardiner said that it might be said that Hitler declared war on the world when he started his brown-shirts marching on German roads. If this interpretation were correct the only country which realized the situation was Russia which turned out to be the only nation ready for the attack. . . .
"In my opinion it was the move of Stalin into Poland in 1939 and not the move of Hitler into Russia in 1,941 which saved Britain," said Mr. Gardiner.
"When the British returned from Dunkirk in 1940, if all the troops in Britain had been given all the arms and ammunition left and commanded to start firing, they could have continued to shoot for one hour."
The preparations made by Stalin compelled Hitler to risk all in an attack upon Russia in the hope he would crush that country before the democracies could arm. . . .
It is quite alright now, in the year 1943, for the Minister of Agriculture or any other hon. member or private citizen of this country to make statements like that; but my contention
is that the people who stated this same fact at the time it happened, in 1939, in other words the communists of this country, were under the defence of Canada regulations rounded up. We all agree now that it was the vast preparations made for war by the Soviet Union which saved Britain and forced Hitler into an attack on the Soviet Union. But as I said before, the people who realized this fact in 1939, and did not wait until 1943 to say it, were arrested under the defence of Canada regulations; they were herded into concentration camps, often with force and violence; they were hounded like common criminals, some of them snatched out of their beds in the middle of the night, and their wives and families had no knowledge where they were to be taken or what was to be done to them.
Some of the Ukrainian people of this country had1 their organization, the Ukrainian Labour-Farmer-Temple association, banned under the defence of Canada regulations, because it was said that certain of them, some leaders among them, were communists. Some of their halls, as you know, were sold. It is a ghastly thing that in some instances their halls were sold to a rival Ukrainian organization whose leaders, though I do not say all the people belonging to it, to say the least had had questionable alliances with pro-fascist terrorist groups in Europe. It is perhaps not very well known that this Ukrainian Labour-Farmer-Temple association had some of its property not, only taken by the custodian of enemy alien property, but actually destroyed by him, instead of being kept. I thought the word "custodian" meant a man who takes things in custody and keeps them until the time arrives to hand them back, but that does not appear to be so. This custodian destroyed property belonging to Ukrainian people in this country whose only fault was that some of the leaders of their organization were supposed to be communists.
I should like to read something which I believe will be of interest to every hon. member, who, before he is Liberal, Conservative or of any other political faith, is a Canadian. I have with me two documents produced by witnesses, sworn statements before notaries, of what happened to some of the property belonging to this organization. It will take only a short time to read them, and I think they should be read:
I,	Steve Solonynka, of the city of Toronto, m the county of York, in the province of Ontario, make oath and say as follows:
1.	I reside at 259 Crawford street, in the city of Toronto, in the county of York.
2.	I have full and personal knowledge of the matters hereinafter by me sworn to except when same are stated to be based upon information and belief.

3.	I was formerly employed by the Pullan Paper Stock Ltd. at Trinity and Parliament streets, in the said city of Toronto, and was employed by the said firm for about five years until about six months ago.
4.	I remember distinctly in the early part of 1941 a load of books, containing about five tons, was brought to the yards of the said company, and the said books were torn and destroyed by the workmen of the said company. These books bore the stamp of the Ukrainian Labour-Farmer-Temple Association.
5.	Many of these books were in the Ukrainian language but many others were in the Russian and English languages.
6.	I remember definitely seeing the following books printed in the English language: works of Victor Hugo, Anatole France, Robert Burns, William Shakespeare, Jack London, Upton Sinclair, Karl Marx, W. Lenin and the History of Canada.
7.	I also remember seeing books printed in the Russian language by Leo Tolstoy, Turgeniew, Maxim Gorki, Pushkin, and books in the Ukrainian language by the following authors: Taras Shewehenko, Ivan Franko, Olga Kobylian-ska, Kulish, Wasil Stefanyk.
8.	While these books were being destroyed by the workmen of the said company, the destruction of same was being supervised by plainsclothes police officers of either the dominion or provincial government.
We have heard about the wholesale destruction of books in Germany. I grew up in a country where no one dictated to me what I should read, and as long as I have breath in my body I will defend the right of the Canadian people to read what they please.
Here is another sworn statement:
I, Mike Andrichuk, of 2272 Wellesly Boulevard, in the city of Windsor, in the province of Ontario, Ford worker, make oath and say as follows,

1.	I am by nationality a Ukrainian and was employed from the middle of the year 1938 to on or about April 1. 1941, as a janitor of the Ukrainian Labour-Farmer-Temple Association Hall at street number 10628 96th street, in the city of Edmonton, in the province of Alberta.
2.	In the said hall at the time of my said employment was a library belonging to the said Ukrainian Labour-Farmer-Temple Association consisting of approximately 1,000 library books some of which were used in a schoolroom and some of which were used for general library purposes amongst the membership of the said association. Amongst the said books were works of Gorki, Marx, Tolstoy and other great Russian writers as well as works in English by Shakespeare, Burns and Winston Churchill. There were also works by Shevchenko, the Ukrainian national poet, and by Jack London.
3.	In or about the month of April, 1941, the said hall was sold by the custodian of enemy property to the Ukrainian National Federation, a pro-fascist organization. By instructions given to me by a Mr. Wenspir and a Mr. Hamilton, representatives of the said custodian, I was
*ordered to burn, and did burn, approximately 500 of the said books in the furnace in the basement of the said hall.

of Burns, surely?

Yes, volumes of Burns were burned.
Sacrilege!

Sacrilege! I should say so.
The said burning took place about one month prior to the sale of the said building and I was further ordered by the said Wenspir and Hamilton to assist in loading the balance of the said books into a truck and the said books were taken by the said truck to the said garbage disposal plant of the city of Edmonton and there destroyed. At the time of the destruction of the said books the same were in good, usable condition. The said Wenspir and Hamilton or an auctioneer were present with me in the basement of the said hall when I began to burn the said 500 of the said books in the basement furnace according to their instructions.
I was being paid by the custodian of enemy property a salary or wage of $35 monthly together with the use of three rooms from the beginning of July, 1940, to April 1, 1941.
The said Wenspir and Hamilton told me that the said books were being destroyed because the custodian did not want the people to be reading them any longer.
Have you ever heard anything like that in a country that calls itself democratic?
The said library was in process of being gathered together over a period of fifteen (15) years and there were from 500 to 700 Ukrainian anti-fascists making use of the said library month by month.
I verily believe that it was a very great cultural hardship to the Ukrainian community in the city of Edmonton to be deprived of the said books, the majority of which were in the Russian and Ukrainian language, which language many of the said community could read much more easily in the said Ukrainian or Russian language.
In addition to the destruction of the said books the said representatives of the custodian's department also conducted an auction sale of some of the furniture and equipment of the said hall, the same being sold to the general public.
I should like to know what evil intelligence thinks that it can dictate to British subjects in this country what they may or may not read. What Goebbelesque monstrosity dares to destroy the works of some of the greatest authors the world has ever known?
I should like to read you another letter. This is pitiful. Its English is not very good but you will understand it:
Dear Mrs. Nielsen:
I am Ann Galangey. I want to bring to your attention the following.
In the midsummer of 1940 the officer of R.C.M.P. raided our house, 13 Clarence, without reading the warrant to search the house, and without any reason they seized a number of literature; among these were number of my music books consist of famous composers of music, despite of my request they have never been returned to me.
Snatching the music books from children under the defence of Canada regulations!

War Appropriation-Justice
History has taught us something. It has taught us that the Ukrainian people do not retreat or surrender to the enemy when they fight. They are among the immortals of the world, and they have died for freedom's sake. Those Ukrainian people in Canada, too, have been fighting against the enemy, not a foreign enemy but the domestic enemy in Canada. They have been fighting, not with force and violence, but with all the forces of democracy which they can muster. They have been fighting with petitions and letters to the government, letters to the Minister of Justice, and it is to our everlasting shame, the shame of members of this House of Commons, that we have not fought harder with them and made their fight our own.
Under these regulations the communist party of this country was banned. Now, every member of this house can think exactly what he pleases about me; I do not care one bit what people think of me. One does not have to be a member of the Salvation Army to agree that the Salvation Army should have the right to exist in this eountiy; one does not have to be a member of the communist party in this day and age to agree that at the present time they should have the ban lifted from them.
Although much has been said in the past abount the Soviet Union, you, my friends, know perfectly well how history has disproved those lies. You remember what was said about communist Russia years ago. I should like to quote something that was said a few years ago about communist Russia. It is not necessary to say who said it because it is the kind of thing that was said by so many people:
The world has learned two important truths about Russia. One is that Stalin is the very spirit of evil incarnate and the other is that the armed might of Russia is a myth.
The equipment in air force, army and navy is plentiful but out of date. The training and morale of the troops is bad. The army and navy have few trained officers and agriculture is badly disorganized. As a nation they are in every respect unfitted to engage any great power.
That is the kind of rubbish we heard circulated around the four comers of the world- lies generated and distilled in the minds of the people by the fascist leaders. They were repeated by fools and knaves all over the world. It was the communists who said that if ever we hope to preserve democracy we should join with the Soviet Union, but that was not published in those days. Just as history has proved all that foolishness to be incorrect, so I am perfectly sure that history will also prove something else to be incorrect, and that is another fallacy and lie
which originated with the same fascist sources. I mean the lie that communists believe in and will use force and violence. I would refer you, my friends, to the brief which was submitted by the communist party of this country to the Rowell-Sirois commission on dominion-provincial relations. It was admitted by unbiased readers at that time to be one of the finest briefs submitted, one of the finest types of analyses ever made of social conditions in Canada. I quote from page 14 of the brief:
The Communist party stands for socialism. But the Communist party repudiates now as in the past all theories or proposals looking to the forcible imposition of socialism upon the majority of the people. Such concepts are utterly and completely foreign to the Communist party. We never did and never will hold to a programme of forcible establishment of socialism against the will of the people. Anyone who proposes the attainment of socialism other than through the democratic will of the people is alien to the Communist party. The Communist programme and policy rests exclusively upon the democratic will of the people. No genuine democrat need harbour any fears of the Communist party.
Let me come to a more recent publication, which I am sure all members must have seen. I refer to the magazine Saturday Night of June 19, in which the leader of the communist party had his life story written up under the title, "Name in the News-How Tim Buck Got That Way". Many prominent men in Canada have had their lives so written up. I quote:
It is the same "Tim Buck", and just as was the case when the Rowell-Sirois commission was sitting, he recently rose before the national war labour board to present the outstandingly finest brief that has been submitted. Its merits lay in its clarity, scholarly documentation, thoroughly adult attitude toward a complex problem on which it endeavoured not to vituperate, but to shed light. It was aimed not at the overthrow of democracy, but at the establishment of a realistic, comprehensive dominion labour code. Mr. Buck produced a document that even the most conservative-minded legal experts in Ottawa consider well worthy of study. . . .
Canada, he says, is so -widely integrated politically that such a measure as is usually credited to him as his objective, namely, a small group grabbing physical power and enforcing communism upon the unwilling mass of citizens, would be quite out of the question. Support of the majority of the people for communism would be necesary in order to enforce it, and this they must show, in our parliamentary system, by voting for those who advocate it.
I should like to remind the house that the truth and only the truth will set us free, even if the truth falls on our ears and sounds strangely after the lies to which we have been accustomed for many years. If any member feels it incumbent upon himself to get up
War Appropriation-Justice

and defend the Minister of Labour in the administration of the defence of Canada regulations-

Not the Minister of
Labour.

The Minister of Justice; I beg your pardon. I hope that no member of this house will insult our intelligence by declaring that the communist party believes in force and violence or will consciously or unconsciously peddle the lies of Hitler and Mussolini in this chamber in this regard. If there are two things more necessary now than ever before they are these. We must win the war for our own sakes, and to do that we need two things. We need international unity and the faith of our allies in us, and we need also national unity and the faith of the Canadian people in the democratic leadership this government should be giving them.
On June 22 of this year I went to Toronto, just as the Prime Minister did, to the great gathering that took place in the Maple Leaf Gardens for the "Salute to Russia," and I listened with considerable pleasure to the speech which he made on that occasion. Let me quote from the speech he made on June 22 as reported in the Globe and Mail of June 24. I quote:
"Apart altogether," he said, "from our comradeship-in-arms there are many reasons why friendship between our two countries should be particularly close," and he foresaw in the promotion of such understanding and friendship between nations "the beginnings of the new world order."
The editorial in the Globe and Mail goes on to say:
The views and sentiments which Mr. King expounded were quite impeccable, and altogether his speech was a commendable performance.
But it was surely a very unfortunate coincidence that on the day Mr. King was hymning the praises of Russia his Minister of Justice was reported as explaining to the House of Commons that he still regarded the Communist party of Canada as an illegal organization, and had no intention of lifting the ban upon it. Now the ruling spirits of the soviet union may have decreed the dissolution of the Comintern, but they have not foresworn communism, and are still in theory firm adherents of that creed.
We hope that Mr. Feodor Gousev, the Russian minister, has a strong sense of humour and can laugh at the farcical coincidence of our Prime Minister's elaborate eulogies of communist Russia and his Minister of Justice's reiteration of his determination to keep the Canadian Communist party suppressed.
What happened at Singapore in the last few tragic days before that city fell? They released the communists from the prisons. Why? Because they knew those people would defend Singapore to the very last drop

of blood in their bodies. When crisis overtook India and there was need for national unity, what was done? The ban on the Communist party was lifted. What is being done now in the efforts to unite the Free French? I quote from the New York Herald-Tribune of June 25, as follows:
The French committee of national liberation at a meeting to-day completed the personnel of the permanent military commission and declared invalid the acts of German-dominated courts in France against French patriots. . . .
The anti-communist laws adopted by the Edouard Daladier government on September 26, 1939, were abrogated and amnesty granted for sentences passed under these laws.
That is fine, but, I ask, who is out of step? Are all the other united nations out of step or are we? Last year wide sections of the Canadian people signed petitions headed "We Stand for Freedom", which appeared as full page advertisements in nearly all the great newspapers across this country. Leading churchmen of the protestant churches have asked, on behalf of themselves and their congregations, for the lifting of the ban on the communist party to promote national and political unity in this period of Canada's war emergency. Professors in our universities; business men; well known people such as Sir Ernest MacMillan, Clifford Sifton and Sir Ellsworth Flavelle; artists; leaders of farm and trade union organizations; Mr. Bracken, on behalf of the Progressive Conservative party of Canada; Liberal members, individually-all have expressed their feeling that this ban should be lifted. Every hon. member is familiar with the recommendation which was brought down in this house last year, but -which has been absolutely ignored since that time. The issue is not whether or not we are in favour of communism; the majority are not, and we all know that. The point is that there are only two alternatives before us to-day; and we must be on either one side or the other. Either we want a united Canada to win the war, with full democratic privileges to all who fight against nazi tyranny, or we are willing to allow a small group in the province of Quebec who oppose full participation in the war, and who do not really represent the people of Quebec, to dominate our government and our Minister of Justice, and to destroy the democracy which is the heritage of the Canadian people.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, democracy is allergic to despotism; it is allergic to the abuse of power. Democracy cannot live in the kind of atmosphere we have in Canada. Either the Minister of Justice obeys the will of the democratic majority of the people of this country or he becomes a despot and misuses

War Appropriation-Justice
the power which has been entrusted to him as a war emergency measure, to protect us from the machinations of the enemy within. It is true-and I hope the Hansard reporter gets this statement correctly-that communists all over the world are a menace. Yes, they are a menace, but to whom? Communists all over the world are a menace to fascists, to fascist-minded people and to those who propagate fascist propaganda. Because of that I say we should allow the communists to fight with us, legally, and should lift the ban upon them in this country. On behalf of the people of Canada my friends, hundreds and thousands of them-the great majority of them, I am convinced-I would ask the Minister of Justice before the end of this session to lift the ban from the communist party and all other democratic groups who have been denied their privileges and rights under the defence of Canada regulations. I ask that he grant them full freedom and give them every opportunity to participate in the winning of the war, or resign his position as Minister of Justice. It may be true that the communists are forming a new organization; there are reports to that effect, but that does not alter the fact that as long as the ban remains on the communist party, all Canadians are in danger; because any time any group of people advocated something with which the Minister of Justice does not agree, it would be the easiest thing in the world for him to say, under the defence of Canada regulations, " Representations have been made to me that you are a communist," and once again we would have a round-up. In Italy and Germany it all started with the rounding up of the communists, but it did not end with that. First the people gave away their rights to protect that minority; then little by little any liberal-minded person who dared express an opinion contrary to that of the powers that were, also found his way-as did Niemoller and thousands of others-into a concentration camp.
These things are not new; you are all familiar with them. I would say to you very definitely that our Minster of Justice has full command of the letter of the law, but in my opinion he has failed dismally to appreciate the spirit of democracy, and never in my life have I said anything about which I was more sincere. He has failed to capture the essential spirit of democracy. I would ask the support of every hon. member of this house; I would ask you to be Canadians first and forget your party; for the party must come second to the fact that we are all Canadians. I would ask that you support the idea that the people
of this country should have the opportunity for full political unity. You will remember that a great deal has been said about how wrong it is for people to join this communist party. Some time ago I noticed an item in the New York Times which was an eye-opener to me, and it may be that other hon. members have not seen it. It came from San Jose in Costa Rica under date of June 20, and reads:
Catholic workers may belong to the new political party, Yanguardia Popular, formerly the communist party, according to Archbishop Victor Sanbria, but catholics may not join nazi or fascist organizations. This information was given by the archbishop to Manual Mora, who was elected to congress by the communist party, of which he was secretary. He is secretary of the new party.
The archbishop indicated that while communism seeks world happiness and economic well being, and respects political, social and religious institutions, catholic workers may belong to Vanguardia Popular. Regarding nazism and fascism the archbishop quoted Father Juan Maria Restrepo Jaramille of Columbia as follows: "No Christian can be a nazi; no Christian can sympathize with nazism."
Perhaps, my friends, some of you may think what I have said to-day is a little stronger than it should have been. There is nothing too strong to be said in defence of those principles of democracy which alone will give us the power to win the war and build the new world in which we all believe so earnestly and for which our men are fighting. It is necessary that within this country we preserve the rights and privileges that belong to all free men and that no small section of our people be denied these things; for if you and I deny to one small section of the people the rights and privileges of democracy, it may be our turn next and, as I said before, when that time comes it will be too late.
Once again I would beg every single member of this house, whatever his party, whatever his position, to forget his party and to remember only one thing, that he is a Canadian and that he believes in democracy. I would urge their support to the end that before this session is concluded the Minister of Justice shall guarantee political unity for the winning of the war by lifting the ban on the communist party and all other democratic parties who have been denied their freedom under the defence of Canada regulations.

Mr. Chairman, I need not tell you that I do not agree with the views of the hon. member for North Battleford. Far from it, I urge the hon. the Minister of Justice to maintain the ban on communism in Canada. We do mot want the communist revolution to cause, soon or later, simultaneous outbreaks in a hundred places,'
War Appropriation-Justice

as happened in the country where that perverse and Godless doctrine originated.
I shall avail myself of this opportunity to call once again the attention of the hon. the Minister of Justice to the imprisonment of Mr. Camillien Houde, former mayor of Montreal and member for Montreal-St. Mary in the Quebec legislative assembly. The arbitrary nature of the prolonged imprisonment of Mr. Camillien Houde is not consistent with the democracy for which Canada is now waging a relentless fight. Neither is it consistent with the principles of freedom which we claim to be upholding in this war, or with the spirit of British criminal law which we have always observed. I will go farther; I do not hesitate to say that the powers given to the Minister of Justice under the defence of Canada regulations mean the sabotaging of our judicial institutions. They mean the discard of the habeas corpus principle, one of the most sacred rights of every British citizen. What is the reason of such relentlessness toward Mr. Houde? Has he not -long since paid his penalty? He has languished during two years and ten months in a concentration camp. He was taken from an internment camp, wearing the prisoners' uniform, and escorted by two constables as if he had been the lowest scoundrel, and he was brought before the advisory board at Fredericton. Tim Buck and his confederates have been freed, as well as Franceschini and others. Why has Camillien Houde not been given his freedom? That is what parliament has a right to know. The return of which I demanded the production a few days ago would certainly have enlightened us on that point. Powers should not be exceeded, Mr. Chairman, and there should be no persecution. So far as I know, that is not included in the war aims of the allies. Neither is it in accordance with the clauses of the Atlantic charter. I shall not say anything more.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few words to say, with a view to securing information respecting the operation of the defence of Canada regulations, this being the only opportunity upon which such information will be forthcoming. I would ask the minister to state how many prosecutions have taken place under the defence of Canada regulations in the past year, how many convictions there have been, and how many searches under the powers of the regulations have been executed in the past year. Furthermore, I believe a general statement on the defence of Canada regulations is due at this time.

If there is one thing to be considered more than another in connection with the administration of regulations which grant extraordinary powers in a time of war, it is that they be administered fairly and in such a way as not to interfere with any person's right of speech, or freedom' of speech, so long as that freedom of speech is not exercised in a manner likely to prove detrimental to the welfare of the state. Furthermore the powers must not be used, nor must there be any suggestion of their being used, to stifle the religious beliefs of any group or body of people in Canada. This, again, subject to the condition that such religious beliefs are not being propagated in such a way as to interfere with the safety and integrity of the state. We go a long way farther under the administration of these regulations than do the British people. At one time the Minister of Justice was president of the Canadian Bar association, and on many occasions before that association he has heard outstanding lawyers from all parts of the dominion request that which I now request, namely, that the administration of these regulations shall be administered so as not to interfere with the religious beliefs of any person. At the last bar association meeting Sir William Monckton, counsellor of the duchy of Lancaster and representative of the British bar to the meeting of the Canadian Bar association, set out the point of view of the British bar and bench respecting the administration of the regulations in England which are analogous in their nature and effect to our defence of Canada regulations. He said this:
Democracy still prevails except where suspended to guard the national safety. When we became involved in this conflict there were many who prophesied that total war would prove incompatible with the essential civil freedoms. When they saw the wide powers which the British government assumed, they warned us that we were in danger of losing our liberty, but it has not been so. We have indeed been glad to give up for the purposes and period of the war a large measure of our freedom to choose our work. But this we recognize as inescapable if, as we wholeheartedly desire, the best use is to be made of our services to win the war.
And these words particularly I bring to the attention of the minister:
On the other hand freedom from capricious arrests and freedom of speech have been sedulously preserved.
That has been the attitude of the British people throughout the war. They deny the right of anyone to endanger the safety of the state, but they preserve freedom from capricious arrest, and freedom of speech.

War Appropriation-Justice
I have in mind the situation with respect to Jehovah's Witnesses. I do not uphold their doctrines, nor their tenets or beliefs. But I do uphold their right to worship their God as they please, so long as they do not thereby interfere with the safety of the state. Last year a committee of parliament recommended the removal of the ban on Jehovah's Witnesses. Yet the ban still remains. The experience of most of us has been that these are harmless people, devoid of any intent to do wrong to the state. Their beliefs are similar to the beliefs of conscientious objectors belonging to other religious groups. Why has the ban not been lifted? It cannot be because of any fear that this organization is detrimental to the welfare of the state, or that its actions are subversive to the war effort. There has never been even the slightest evidence that such is the case. If my recollection is correct, a number of outstanding lawyers in this dominion have made the statement that there was no such danger from this body. Why has the ban not been lifted? Why are these people still considered to be criminal simply because of the fact that they worship their god according to the tenets of their belief?
I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a matter which was brought to my attention within the last four or five days, a matter which I think requires some explanation. A woman by the name of Mrs. H. H. Mullins, of St. Georges de Beauce, in the province of Quebec, endeavoured to distribute some literature. I have a couple of samples of the type of literature she was distributing. It is in French, but I translate:
The Holy Bible is the Word of God. Read it.
Then follow a number of quotations from the New Testament according to the Crampon version. There is nothing in this literature other than quotations from the Holy Bible. But what happened to her? Around the fourth of this month the R.C.M.P. entered her premises. I speak subject to correction by the minister in what I shall say of the facts, but my information is that they made a search. They entered and removed the literature she had been distributing. There is nothing in the literature other than quotations from the Holy Bible. Is there anything in that type of literature that is detrimental to the welfare of the state or subversive in any way? While I have not the charge here, I am informed it was that she was distributing literature upon which the printer's name did not appear. This literature contains quotations from St. Paul's Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 1, verse 3; the Epistle of Paul to the Romans, chapter 15, verse 4; the second Epistle of Paul to Timothy, chapter 3, verse 16, and so on. On July
8 this woman was taken into custody and placed in the gaol. I do not know what has happened to her since. I think an explanation is due as to why this search took place and why this woman was incarcerated instead of being brought before the court by summons. Most proceedings may be commenced under the defence of Canada regulations, but they cannot be continued unless the attorney general of the province or a representative of the Minister of Justice concurs. These are things which require the strictest consideration by parliament, because parliament exists for the purpose of redressing wrongs. Are prosecutions still taking place of Jehovah's Witnesses? If so, why are these prosecutions taking place? Why have the defence of Canada regulations not been amended in accordance with the recommendation of the defence of Canada regulations committee, which was composed of distinguished lawyer members of this house and men of experience from every province in the dominion? One year after this recommendation was made it is apparently still an offence to belong to an evangelical body, even though that body is preaching doctrines which none of us believe, I ask the minister to explain these things.

Mr. Chairman, what I am going to refer to to-day I have referred to before, and as I do not want to hold up the committee I shall not make any extended remarks. This committee has before it now a matter which has been before parliament since we adjourned at the end of last session, and I think it is something on which we should give an expression of opinion. It seems to me that the action of the Department of Justice cr of the government is not in accord with democratic procedure. I refer to the lifting of the ban of illegality which was imposed on certain organizations in June, 1940. A number cf organizations are included in this group, among them being the communist party of Canada, There are other organizations which might be termed subsidiaries or affiliates of this organization, and which were declared illegal because of their connection with the communist partjr. There is also the sect referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), Jehovah's Witnesses. I make a plea to-day for the lifting of the ban on the communist party. I am sure that no one in this house will accuse me of being a member of that party or of having any association with it. I have had to contest three elections to this house and on each occasion I have been opposed by a member of the communist party. At times they have not minced their words in opposing me, it having been stated that my election would really be
War Appropriation-Justice

more of a detriment to the interests of the workers than would the election of a member ox one of the old-time parties. Up until now my constituents have not agreed with that point of view.
The communist party of Canada was in existence before June, 1940, when it was declared illegal. Up until that time it had carried on its activities in the same way as other organizations. If it went beyond the laws of the country, those laws were there to check either the party or the individual member. It was declared an illegal organization in June, 1940, not because of anything in its constitution but because of its opposition to the war. That is why it and other organizations with it, were declared illegal. They advocated opposition to the war. As a matter of fact the candidate of the communist party opposing me in the election of 1940 opposed me because I was, he said, a warmonger who 'was supporting an imperialist war. There would be sufficient justification to declare such an organization illegal, because we cannot allow people who are opposed to the country's war effort to obstruct that war effort. I am sure that anyone speaking here to-day in favour of lifting the ban on the communist party would say that any organization or any individual who opposed the country's war effort should be put under restraint.
The communist party's attitude to the war, not only here but in every part of the world, remained the same until June 22, 1941. I am not greatly impressed by the suggestion that that sort of attitude saved us from destruction at the hands of the nazis and the fascists. It is my opinion that, if the democracies of the world had accepted the policy of the communist party, Hitler would have overrun the world long before now-let us make no mistake about that.
I was saying that the communist party was declared an illegal organization for a certain reason, and that reason was that the communists were opposed to the war. But now, having changed their opposition to support of the war, I maintain that any reason that existing for declaring the communist party to be an illegal organization has disappeared. I can see no possible reason for maintaining that attitude other than a certain prejudice against communist doctrines. I am myself opposed to communist party philosophy. Nevertheless I submit that as Canadians we cannot maintain that position and still hold that we are democrats, that we are trying to save democracy with all that word implies. Canada is the only member of the British

commonwealth, so far as I am aware, in which
restrictions are imposed on1 the communist party.
May I submit this, that even if the ban was lifted, the country would not be exposed to any danger, because the Minister of Justice would still have just as much jurisdiction in the matter as he had before. There :are laws in this country outside of the defence of Canada regulations to take care of subversive activities. Even under the defence of Canada regulations the minister could act. I have taken that position since the change in the communist party's attitude to the war. In November, 1941, at the first opportunity I had in this house, I proposed that the government should seek an exchange of representatives with the Soviet Union. I am glad that the government has done that. Although it is not a question at issue now', I am satisfied, because of the attitude of the communist party to the Soviet Union, that good relations between the democracies of the world and the Soviet Union is one of the ways by which we can assure orderly change through democratic procedure.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I did not quite catch that last sentence. Did I understand my hon. friend to say that good relations with the Soviet Union were necessary for the establishment of international order, that such relations would be promoted by the relations of the communist party to the Soviet Union?
Mr. MaeINNIS:	That is what I intended
to say, whether I put it clearly enough or not; and for this reason. The actions of the communist party since the war began are clear proof of the fact that they accept Russia as their fatherland. They have no regard for the countries in which they live. Their whole policy is concerned with safeguarding the interests of the Soviet Union. I submit that the way they undertook to do that at the beginning of the war was wrong. If I were a communist I do not think I would have taken that position, because once Great Britain was defeated-let me make this clear -once Great Britain was defeated I do not believe there was any other country on earth that could save the Soviet Union from being overrun by Germany. The difficulties are great enough as they are now, and if Great Britain were defeated to-day the Soviet Union could not be saved from Hitlerism. I realized that at the time, in the same way as I felt within me that the only assurance, the only hope of attaining the kind of world I had

War Appropriation-Justice
worked for these many years, could not be realized without the defeat of Hitler and all that he stands for.
There are other organizations, such as the Ukrainian Labour-Farmer-Temple association, whose properties were confiscated, and in some cases sold, and as the hon. member for North Battleford has said, had their property destroyed. People do that sort of thing. Some people for one reason or another have a violent antipathy to knowledge and understanding, and at the first opportunity they seek to destroy it, just as Hitler sought to destroy the culture of Germany by destroying all that was constructive in the literature of Germany. There are many countries the people of which are not given access to the literature of the rest of the world. We are not working in the interests of Canadian unity now by treating the Ukrainian Labour-Farmer-Temple association as an illegal organization. We are not working to extend unity in our country if we refuse to take whatever action is in our power to return their property to the people who formerly owned it.
May I point out to the Minister of Justice and to the government that there is grave danger of our going off on the wrong track in another matter. I refer to the property of persons of Japanese origin who were moved from the defence area on the Pacific coast. I know it is not popular in certain quarters to say a word for these people; nevertheless I am going to say it. I believe the Minister of Justice and the government are proceeding on a most dangerous course, a course a democracy should not take. These people, with a very few exceptions, were not moved because of charges made against them. A great many of them are Canadian citizens, either by birth or by naturalization, and although they were moved as a defence precaution, we are dealing with their property exactly as though they were enemy aliens, which they are not. I draw that to the attention of the minister, because it is most important.
I support the hon. member for Lake Centre in what he said regarding Jehovah's Witnesses. These people presented their case to the defence of Canada regulations committee last year, and the Department of Justice also presented its case-if you can call it a case- against them. As I have said here before, never have I seen a weaker document upon which to declare an organization illegal than the document which was placed before the defence of Canada regulations committee last year as a justification of the action against Jehovah's Witnesses. I get letters almost every week from members of this sect who
are being molested by the police while exercising their religious rights. I do not care what a person's religion is, or whether he has any religion at all; that is his business and nobody else's; as long as in the exercise of his beliefs he does not interfere with the rights and liberties of others, he is entitled to hold whatever beliefs he sees fit. I should like to see the Minister of Justice, before this house prorogues, do what should have been done a year ago, namely, lift the ban on all these organizations. Then if any action has to be taken, the minister has all the scope for action which the safety of the country requires.

As a member of the defence of Canada regulations committee last year and this year, may I express the views which I hold and which are held also, I believe, by the party of which I am a member. Last year the committee went carefully into this whole subject. They held a good many meetings, they had before them champions of these various organizations and heard the best arguments which they could submit. I do not think I shall be telling tales out of school if I say that I reported to the party I represent-for, believing in democracy as we do, I was not desirous of acting on the committee merely on my own behalf, but sought instructions from our party-and they told me that I should vote on that committee for the lifting of the ban on Jehovah's Witnesses, Technocracy Inc., and the Communist party. I say that and in the same breath say that I do not think anyone in Canada could accuse the Social Credit party anywhere of being communists. That was done because we believe in the rights of free assembly and free speech in a democratic country. The lifting of this ban would not prevent action being taken against any individual who spoke or acted as though he were an enemy of the state. That goes without saying. The police can pick up anyone, whether an unattached individual or a member of any organization, if he is assumed to make utterances or do things which obviously or otherwise are detrimental to the safety of the state. But the fact that people are not free to assemble themselves as they choose, whether for public worship or the discussion of issues, is something which we regard as the very antithesis of democratic freedom.
The communist party, of course, has been referred to a good deal in this connection. However, it is only one of the organizations the ban on which is recommended by the committee to be lifted. Take Jehovah's Witnesses, for instance. I cannot for the life of me see why, because a body of people

War Appropriation-Justice

hold an interpretation of scripture which is adverse to war, the whole body of them should be declared illegal. If we carry that theory to its ultimate conclusion, probably the Doukhobors should be declared an illegal body. They do not believe in war. They do not fight. The evidence was brought out in the defence of Canada regulations hearings that very many adherents of Jehovah's Witnesses were and are in the king's uniform fighting for the country. Are we going to say that Jehovah's Witnesses are enemies of this state? I do not believe they are. I believe they are loyal citizens with a certain religious belief. They are honourable citizens and I see no reason why such an organization should be banned.
I am not here pleading the cause of Jehovah's Witnesses as a religious body because I am not one. As I have said over and over again in this chamber, I do not believe in their religious doctrines, but I do believe that every individual in this country has a right to interpret the scriptures as he desires. People have the right to meet on the Lord's day and assemble for worship as they desire. To say that such people are enemies of the state becauses they hold a certain belief is nonsense. I might just as well say that the pacifist in 1939 and since then has been and is now equally an enemy of the state. I might as well say that those who voted for a reduction in the defence estimates right up until almost the time of the war are as much enemies of the state as Jehovah's Witnesses. I believe they are enemies of the state. They did more harm to the country in sabotaging the country to the enemy than did Jehovah's Witnesses. These people are not regarded to-day as enemies of the state, however; they are honourable citizens holding certain convictions. That is all. I simply bring that to the attention of the committee.
One thing more I would say and that is in regard to the government's refusal to accept the recommendations of the committee. They had a perfect right to do so. It was within their purview; it was within their authority to refuse to accept the recommendations. But obviously it was a reflection upon the work of that committee. Unquestionably it was. The committee had all the evidence and it comprised men of average intelligence in this house, and those men arrived at their conclusions. To refuse to accept their recommendations can be regarded pretty much as a slap in the face.
I am not going to make a charge, but I am wondering how that committee will vote on the same question this year if they get a

chance to vote on it. The committee was not set up until well on in the session, and when it was set up the meeting of the committee was delayed and delayed until it was only a few weeks ago that they began their sittings. Somebody is responsible for that. At one of the first meetings we had a communication was read. I believe it was from Mr. Tim Buck; at any rate, it was either from him or from his organization. That communication requested that they be heard. I do not know whether they will be heard. Of course, the minister can say, "You are a member of the committee; why don't you insist on its being done?"

I do not like to
interrupt the hon. member, but I suggest that his remarks are not in order at this time. As he has said, he is a member of the committee and I assume that in due course the committee will make a report, and the matter can be discussed then. But there is a standing order which prohibits the discussion of the work of a committee until it has made its report. My second objection, with which I think the hon. member will agree, is that this is hardly pertinent to the matter now under discussion here.

I realize that one cannot discuss the work and the report of the committee that is still sitting, but my point is this. We are asked to vote a sum of money for the operation of the defence of Canada regulations. The committee of last year made recommendations, and those recommendations were not acted upon, and now we are asked to vote a further sum. All I am asking is this. If the committee this year brings in the same recommendations, will they be acted upon? The minister is not going to answer that question, I know, because he cannot do so now; but I am not now discussing the report of the committee. I am discussing the fact that the committee has been delayed in its operations, for some reason or other, and something should be done about it before it is too late. The committee is set up to deal with the defence of Canada regulations. Here is an appropriation we are asked to vote for the operation of the department under those regulations.
I will conclude by reiterating that what we are concerned about is to preserve the democratic right of free assembly and free speech in Canada. I think it does more harm than good to stop free speech, because when you stop free speech you do not know what is going on in the people's minds. When they are permitted to say what they think,

War Appropriation-Justice
we know where these various bodies stand. We know what this man or that man believes because he is permitted to express it. But how can you deal with anything properly and effectively if it is not permitted any expression? You cannot do it; that is all. I submit that to this committee and I urge that the recommendations be acted upon. It is not too late for the minister to follow that course.

I was not able to catch all that the hon. member said, but so far as they relate to Jehovah's Witnesses I endorse his remarks. I hope that if the minister is not disposed to make some concession to these people he will be in a position to inform the house and the country very definitely as to some reasonable reason why the ban should be continued against them. No man will support the minister more loyally than I in regard to anything he may do to suppress activities of a subversive character, but I know a number of these people, I live not far from them, and I have never known of any disloyalty among them, nor do I know anyone else who had any charge of that kind to make against Jehovah's Witnesses. They happen to have peculiar religious beliefs with which I do not agree, but that does not make them harmful or subversive. They may condemn my religious beliefs, and while, in times like these, we must be careful not to permit any underground work to go on under popular names, at the same time it is equally essential in these days when we are fighting for freedom that we should not go to the other extreme and penalize people unless we are sure that their doctrines or the methods they propose for carrying those doctrines into effect are subversive.
So far as my considerable knowledge of these people goes, I can say that there are a number of them in the district I represent and that they are decent, respectable people. Whatever their religious beliefs may be, that is beside the point. If the minister is not willing to take the ban off, I wish he would give us something to carry home to our people so that they may know why their organization is banned. It sometimes happens that while what you might call the ordinary people are quite blameless in their actions, some of the heads of the organization, perhaps in a foreign country, have done things which were improper. If that is so, let us know it; at least let us have something that will justify-if the ban is to be continued- the action taken by the government.

Since I was the first
member of this house to recommend the recognition of soviet Russia and the establishment of diplomatic relations, I cannot allow this debate to continue without saying a word or two in regard to this matter. First I will quote just one sentence from what I had to say in February, 1942, with regard to the soviet philosophy; it appears at page 299 of Hansard for that year:
We are going to have to admit that the soviet philosophy exists and that it has done great things; let us admit it openly and above the broad tables of government rather than have snivelling, subversive agents peddling anarchist literature to the adolescent minds of the students in our schools, universities and training camps. We have seen what anarchy has done in other countries. It can happen here.
We are the only part of the British empire to prohibit the communist party. The question of lifting the ban now has become a political football, and I do not propose to discuss that question to-day. I stand by everything I said in 1942, but I should like to say a word or two about communism. The history of the communist party during this war, outside Russia, has been almost what might be called ludicrous. At first they said this was an imperial war, a war for capitalists; it was this kind and that kind of a war, until Russia was attacked. Now the same people who urged young men in our training centres to have nothing to do with the war are saying this is a holy war. But all that does not mean that communism is not a world force and must not be considered as such. To try to pretend that this force does not exist is to be an ostrich, to bury our heads in the sand. That is what I object to in the present policy of the government. When France fell, one of the most disturbing features of the destruction of the French army-and this is particularly true of the army in the south- was the fact that it was riddled with communism. Statement after statement has been made by French soldiers who said, "The first thing we did when the Germans attacked was to shoot our officers. Then we did not know what to do." That was the effect of communism.
But what has it done in Russia? The study of Russian history and of Russia itself is something that should be taken out of the realm of politics. We study the French revolution; we study all the revolutions that have occurred in the history of the world including the one during which Charles I was executed. There is every reason why the same study should be given to the Russian revolution that has been going on since 1917, no matter what we may
War Appropriation-Justice

think of it or how we may disagree with certain of its tenets. To try to gloss over the facts; to keep this movement under cover, in my opinion creates a great danger to this state, and that is why I oppose the policy of the government. I am wholly and absolutely against communism, but it is a world power, a great movement, and we must recognize it as such. Let us not cover it up; let us bring it into the open, so that we may understand what it is. Let us not have one man saying that the salvation of the world depends upon communism and the man opposite saying that communism is the worst possible thing that ever happened to Russia. Let us evaluate the thing; let us get the proper facts; let us make a study of them; let us bring it into the open, so that we may all see what we axe dealing with.

I have in my riding many Ukrainians, of whom there are large numbers in the city of Toronto. They belong to various associations, one of which is called the U.L.F.T.A. I know many of these people personally. It may be that at the beginning of the war they were communists; I do not know what they are now. They seem to be good citizens, or at least I believe they could be made into good citizens. In June, 1940, their organization was declared illegal and all its properties became vested in the custodian of alien property. They tell me that no formal charges were made by the government at any time, and that aside from the language of regulation 39C of the defence of Canada regulations they were given no indication as to why the ban was imposed. That regulation reads:
The following associations, societies, groups or organizations are hereby declared to be, and shall be deemed to be, illegal organizations. . . .
I imagine they were against the war and that was why the ban was imposed at that time. However, I understand that a change has taken place in the interval. All their properties were confiscated. In Toronto they had a very fine building which had been erected with the nickles, quarters, fifty-cent pieces, dollars and hard work of the people themselves. It was unfortunate that they got under communist control. Perhaps at that time the confiscation of their property was the right thing to do, but the mistake was in selling that property. As I understand it, other property belonging to Germans, Italians and Japanese is still held by the custodian of alien property, but in this case a different procedure was followed. As a matter of fact, I believe many of the members

of this association were Canadian citizens at the time. They had been here for a long time, and had taken their part in the development of Canadian music, and various Canadian activities. As I say, their property was confiscated. There were many protests in the newspapers, and from the civil liberties' association. Things have changed since then. What is the government going to do about the situation? I say that the fact that these properties are sold, and not held for them, is a great injustice. Are they to be treated forever as outcasts, and their property kept away from them, or is some restitution to be made to them, in the event of their behaving themselves and becoming good Canadian citizens.
While I am on my feet there is another matter to which I should like to refer. I suggest there should be a more elaborate ceremony in connection with naturalization proceedings. When a man or a woman takes upon himself the responsibilities of citizenship, he or she is accepting a heavy responsibility.

speakeroldname: The ACTING CHAIRMAN (Mr. Ross, Calgary East):
speechtext: May I direct the attention of the hon. member to the fact that the item before the committee deals with expenditures in connection with the administration of the defence of Canada regulations.
I understand that.

speakeroldname: The ACTING CHAIRMAN (Mr. Ross, Calgary East):
speechtext:
I hope the hon. member will confine himself to the item.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The hon. member will have a full opportunity to discuss naturalization when the civil estimates of the Secretary of State, under whose department naturalization is administered, are before the committee. This department has nothing whatsoever to do with it.

Has not this question connected with taking property away from these people something to do with it?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes; but the hon. member was discussing naturalization.

Perhaps the committee would permit me to complete what I began to say. I believe there should be a more elaborate ceremony for naturalization. It should be more impressive. I point out, too, that those people who are good Canadian citizens, who have been deprived of their property, who have been banned, and all that sort of thing, are still good Canadian citizens, and they should have proper consideration.

War Appropriation-Justice
Hon. N. A. McLA.RTY (Secretary of State): Mr. Chairman, in view of the discussion which has taken place in connection with the custodian, it might be proper for me to say a few words. I do not intend to speak at length. It just so happens that while I have been custodian it was not necessary either to destroy a book or to sell a single piece of property. So far as books are concerned, I had no information as to what books, if any, were destroyed. And, as a result of the question placed upon the order paper a few days ago by the hon. member for North Battleford, we have written to ascertain whether a list was made at the time the books were destroyed, at both Edmonton and Toronto. The hon. member's observations this afternoon were the first intimation I had that any books whatsoever had been destroyed at Toronto, and I have not had an opportunity to investigate upon that point.
However, I did investigate the situation in regard to the sale of the labour temples. I believe that out of 111 some seventeen have been sold. But my advice is that not a single labour temple which was able to carry itself was sold. This is not a dominion-wide organization; and I mean by that that one cannot transfer funds from a central source to protect the individual temples. Each temple had to stand on its own feet.	.
Now, not one single labour temple was sold, except for one of three causes: First, there was a mortgage against it, and usually heavily overdue. The revenue was not sufficient to pay the mortgage. In that event foreclosures would inevitably have followed, and the whole thing would have been a complete loss. Second, there were other cases in which there were heavy arrears of taxes. If sales had not been made in respect of those cases, again there would have been complete loss to the owners. Third, some of the buildings were in an extremely dilapidated condition. There were no funds of that branch available to put them in proper condition, and they were becoming more dilapidated day by day. In other words, before any property was sold, at least one of those conditions had to exist.
In connection with the sales, I am advised that none were sold without advertisements for tenders being carried in the newspapers. In all cases I believe tenders were asked for. Then they could not be sold to any organization which stood in the same position as the owners of the temples.
I mention these facts so that the public may not gain the impression that the custodian was out to try to effect sales. That is not correct. The only sales effected were to preserve the equity which might exist in the property which will, when the ban is lifted,
be returned to those who are entitled to receive it. In other words, I am advised the custodian did not look for purchasers. He was not anxious to sell it, and in fact where it paid its own way, had no carrying charges and would not be a complete loss, he refused to sell it. I think hon. members in the committee will agree that where the assets were wasting, it was much better to realize what could be realized, rather than just let it go by default, and realize nothing at all.
I believe that is the whole situation in connection with the sale of labour temples. They were not sold because the custodian wanted to sell them. They were sold because, if he did not sell them, there would not be anything left for the owners.
It is needless for me to point out that the custodian was and is a purely administrative officer. The government of Canada placed the ban, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice of the day. Once that was done, the custodian did not act under section 39 of the defence of Canada regulations. The custodian acts-must act-under the authority of the trading with the enemy regulations. Consequently, I should like to make it abundantly clear that I am not arguing for the return of the property to the labour temples. Frankly, I am told it would be a relief to the custodian if they were returned, because they have been a considerable burden and care. But I do wish to make the position clear, because the suggestion was made that we were simply trying unfairly to rid ourselves of the temples, by selling. That is not correct.
Mr. STIRLING; Would the Secretary of State be good enough to refer to a subject discussed by the hon. member for Vancouver East, namely the sale of Japanese property. Is it correct to say that no Japanese properties have been disposed of, except with the consent of the owners?

No; that is not correct. I do not think the consent of the owners was ever requested in respect of the rural property sold to the soldier settlement board. In that connection may I explain that we set up two advisory committees. One was to deal with urban properties, and was headed by Mr. Justice Sydney Smith; and the other, headed by Judge Whiteside, was to deal with rural properties. Japanese sat on each of these committees. One felt, however-and I believe one could scarcely criticize him for the feeling- that they were being placed in an extremely embarrassing position. The result was that he resigned. But to say that we got the consent of all the owners in connection with the sale of 769 parcels to a value of $850,000
War Appropriation-Justice

would not be correct. What happened was that the sale was negotiated by the local representative of the custodian acting in the first instance, and Mr. McPherson acted in the second. The price was tentatively agreed upon. It was then submitted to the advisory committee, and the advisory committee unanimously recommended its acceptance. Those are the only properties of Japanese evacuees which, so far as I know, have been sold.
