No; we would expect the minister to reply.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am waiting until hon. members have concluded their remarks.

On July 7 the minister gave certain information in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for North Battle-ford (Mrs. Nielsen) and referring to Charles Brandel Crate, who was designated as the former leader of the Canadian Union of Fascists. I was greatly surprised that this statement should have been made, inasmuch as the- impression was conveyed that this man, who had become quite famous prior to the outbreak of war on account of his assertions against the democratic form of government, had been allowed to go free simply because he had dissociated himself, so to speak, from the organization by signing a declaration to the effect that he was no longer a subversive agent dangerous to Canada and to our form of government. I am just wondering how many cases there are where a similar situation developed. Following the signing of the declaration, Crate was employed in Newfoundland, then by a Toronto construction company and later on he went to Dawson Creek in British Columbia. Whether this man reported periodically to the mounted police is something about which I am not certain, but I have reason to believe that he did not. I understand that for three months prior to June 1 the Royal Canadian Mounted Police lost track of this individual.
I happened to meet Crate quite by accident early in June. I did not know the man; I had never met him before, but I soon realized what he was on account of the assertions he made at that time. Crate is definitely an exponent of fascist and nazi principles. He makes no bones about that. He stated definitely within my hearing that the only mistake he made was to permit his organization to be designated as a fascist organization. He said that one of the finest things that ever happened to him was when the government of Canada had been led to

believe that the Canadian Union of Fascists no longer existed. He laughed about that. He stated to me that much effective work had been carried on since the banning of the organization in June, 1940. He agreed that the things which Hitler and Mussolini were endeavouring to do were proper things to be done, not only in those countries but here in Canada. He stated that he disagreed to a certain extent with some of the methods used, but he did not disagree in any sense with their objectives.
I think this committee is entitled to information, not only with respect to Crate and Crate's organization but also with respect to the treatment which has been accorded such persons who established reputations in this country prior to the war as fascists or nazis. I do not wish to say more at this time, but I am definitely not satisfied with the statement the minister gave to the house on July 7, 1943.

Did the police receive copies of letters written by Mr. Crate to people in northern Ontario some time last summer in which he definitely stated his intentions to carry on his fascist activities?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I shall make inquiry, but I think I can say at once that the police did not receive such letters. I recently examined the file in the department concerning this man and I saw no evidence of any such letters. Perhaps the hon. member would be kind enough to give me further identifying particulars which would facilitate the inquiry. Perhaps I may be allowed to deal with the matters raised by hon. members not quite in the order in which they were submitted, but taking the last first and the first last. The information supplied by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) about the statements which he himself heard will be of much interest to the police, because this man Crate is at present being prosecuted. I am sure the attorney general of the province in which he is being prosecuted will be glad to know that he will be able to get evidence from the hon. member which may be pertinent to the prosecution.

I think the minister will find that this was shortly before Crate's apprehension. It may be that he was apprehended as a consequence of certain things he said at that time.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Possibly, and that will make them all the more interesting to the attorney general. He will be glad to know that not only will the hon. gentleman be

War Appropriation-Justice
available himself as a witness but will be able to supply the names of other persons who were present.

I am perfectly willing to support any assertions I have made to-day.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am not implying the contrary in any way. This information will be communicated to the attorney general and to the police who have been investigating the situation. It is said that this man was allowed to work in Newfoundland and in Dawson Creek, but these were not protected areas and being a Canadian citizen he would be allowed to go to these places as long as he was not interned. The hon. member asked for information about the members of this party.
I may say that of the thirty or so who were detained, fewer than ten have been released. In the case of other groups that were interned since the outbreak of the war, more than half have been released.
There seems to be some misapprehension with respect to the defence of Canada regulations. I have heard it said several times that the Minister of Justice was to be asked to lift the ban on the Communist party and other subsidiary organizations. That implies power and jurisdiction in the Minister of Justice which he does not have. These regulations were brought into being by the governor general in council. All the Minister of Justice could do would be to recommend to his colleagues in the first instance, and if he got their approval, then a recommendation could be made to his excellency for the modification of the regulations. A recommendation was brought in by a committee toward the end of the session last year, but no attempt was made to have that recommendation adopted by the house. Had it been adopted by the house, it would have been the duty of the Minister of Justice to recommend its implementation. It was well known to members of the house last year that there was serious doubt as to what would have happened to the recommendation had it been put to a vote.

The Minister of Justice does not suggest for a moment that a condition precedent to government action is that the house should take action?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Not at all. I am answering the reproach that I disregarded the view or recommendation of this house. I have not been here long, but I have been here long enough to conceive-that was true even before I came here-such a respect for the house that I should not like to be put in that position. I should not like anyone to feel that I would
attempt to set up my own views against those of the majority of the house. But from what knowledge I had of what took place last year I did not feel that it was the view of the majority of the house that this recommendation should be implemented, and I felt I was at perfect liberty to wait until the house had expressed its views upon it.
There were other matters. I did give consideration to the way in which these regulations were drawn. Hon. members know, of course, that I was not here when they were originally set up. They were in such form that it might appear they imposed restrictions upon religious liberty, and I recommended to my colleagues, and in turn it was submitted to his excellency and approved, that the regulations be amended in such a way as to provide that no person shall be guilty of an offence against the regulations by reason only of his attending a meeting the sole purpose of which is religious worship or instruction.

That does not cover the situation at all. It used to be prima facie evidence of guilt, and this just removes the evidence of guilt and nothing else.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: My learned friend will have an opportunity of criticizing what we did.
I want to give a factual statement of what was done.
There was a further amendment made which could properly be open to the criticism my hon. friend has just suggested. Formerly anyone who was an officer or member belonging to one of these organizations was guilty of an offence. This was amended to provide that anyone "who acted" as an officer or a member would be guilty of an offence under the defence of Canada regulations, subject, of course, to the provision that it would not be an offence against the regulations to attend a meeting for the purpose of worship or instruction. That is -the factual situation, and it is the only point I wish to make at this time.
As to why the ban was originally imposed upon Jehovah's Witnesses, among other organizations, I have only hearsay information about -that, because the regulations wtere passed at -the very outbreak of the war, and this particular provision was adopted in June, 1940, a year and half before I left my professional activities in the city of Quebec. I have ascertained, however, that this is a very large international organization and the amount of literature that is put out from the Watch Tower on behalf of this organization is something fabulous; it runs into tens of millions of tracts and various other publications. It is also well known that thousands
War Appropriation-Justice

of phonographs with recorded speeches of their great leader, the so-called Judge Rutherford, are being used to further enlighten the people. There are also, or there were, very large numbers of motor trucks fitted out with these phonographs and loud speakers to blare to the population at large the merits of that particular doctrine and the demerits of all religions. All religions, according to their theory, are satanic missions to establish and maintain the dominion of his satanic majesty over the whole earth. I do not imagine that was the reason why the regulation was originally enacted, but rather because their doctrine is, of course, against war. There is no war, according to their theory, that is anything but the machinations of the devil himself, and not only that, but their view is that human-made laws have no binding force upon the individual if they happen to contravene what these gentlemen regard as being proper human behaviour. This doctrine is certainly subversive of organized society.

Does it go quite that far?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am informed that it does.
I did not think it did.

The United States supreme court did not find that.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Not on the evidence submitted. The supreme court, of course, had to deal only with the evidence that had been properly submitted in the case. That is the danger of the thing we are now being asked to do, that when you do not make the affirmation that a thing is illegal, the reverse is often asserted as being the effect of that decision, and what has been sought with respect to communists and all these others is something upon which they could declare that this house or this parliament had declared the party to be a legal organization.
With respect to the Ukrainian Farmer-Labour-Temple association and the Finnish organization, they were two incorporated bodies which were used by the communist party as the holding companies for all property acquired for the purposes of the communist party, and the situation with respect to those two organizations is the same as it is with respect to the party itself. No one will attempt to justify the burning of books. I do not know when or where or how that came about. The Department of Justice had nothing to do with the property of the banned organizations. The Secretary of State as custodian is a trustee accountable' for the
fMr. St. Laurent.]
property temporarily vested in him as the result of the banning of an organization or the detention of an individual.

What department ordered the destruction of these books? Their destruction must have been ordered by somebody. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police would not act without instructions.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not know how, when or where it was ordered or even that it was ordered or that it was done, other than the information submitted through the reading of affidavits this afternoon by the hon. member for North Battleford. No one would attempt to defend the burning or destruction of property, whether it be books, music or anything else; and if the property has not been cared for properly by the custodian, he will in due course be required to account for his administration as a trustee of this property.

Have no letters reached the department from groups, such as the Ukrainian Farmer-Labour-Temple association, stating these things?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: There have been hundreds, thousands of letters and petitions, very often on mimeographed forms, indicating clearly that they came from one central spot and were the result of propaganda to achieve the object being pursued. But the hon. member will pardon me if I do not believe, everything which is written in that kind of material which comes to the department.
As regards the communist party and the eloquent address we listened to earlier this afternoon, the reminder that they were the people who were saying in 1939 the things which everybody else is saying in 1943 or was saying in 1942, I have material which is in language as brilliant, as striking, as forceful as the language used by the hon. member to-day, and I would call the attention of the committee to some of it. It is from the election manifesto of the communist party of Canada.

What year?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: In 1940, or subsequent to 1939. I think it was probably in relation to the election to which the hon. member for Vancouver East made some reference in his remarks this afternoon.
They are conniving with the imperialist warlords of Europe to make war against the Soviet Union, the land of socialism, so feared and hated by the blood-drenching rulers of decayed capitalism. Because of this plan, they have been advised by Chamberlain to hold a quick election. . . .
The King government and the capitalist warmongers intend to use this fake election to extend their lying propaganda about the war. . . .

War Appropriation-Justice
In this war, the Canadian capitalists plan to revel in luxury at home, raking in the mounting piles of profits, while sending our best sons to rot and die in the trenches of someone else's war on a far-off continent. Greedily they count the millions that they will make from the life of every Canadian boy sacrificed on their barbarous altar of profits. A degenerate, besotten, parasitical class, they are carrying on a traffic in death. In exchange for war orders they are bartering Canadian lives. . . .
Then, summing up the platform:
. . . Bring Canadian boys back to Canada! Not a man must leave Canada's shores to die in imperialist war!
Repeal of the War Measures Act! The real fight for democracy is here in Canada against the war dictatorship of reaction! Freedom for the honest working class press! Release Douglas Stewart of the Clarion! . . .
The communist candidates, fearlessly taking their stand upon this platform of your interests appeal for your support. Capitalism and the capitalist class, breeding crisis, poverty and the horrible slaughter of war, are your enemies, are the enemies of humanity. . . .
Unite your ranks, build up your popular united front to defeat the war offensive _ upon your living standards and democratic rights! Never submit to the virtual military dictatorship that has been established by capital! Not all their lies, nor all their persecution apd suppression can defeat you!
Do not leave your fate and the destiny of your country in the hands of the parasitic, war-making capitalist class and their politicians! Determine to fight and live in Canada for peace and social progress; not suffer and die for profits! Extricate Canada from the imperialist war! . . .
Go to the polls and cast your votes for the communist candidates, for those who fight for your interests against the imperialist war camp! . . .
Join in one common front against this most criminal war of human history. Strike a blow in this federal election to save Canada, to end the war, for peace!
That is the kind of stuff which was being broadcast throughout Canada at a time when most of the Canadian people were realizing that the security and the very existence of the country were at stake, and a ban was placed by the defence of Canada regulations upon the organization whose views were thus expressed. These regulations were afterwards brought to the House of Commons, were considered and received the approval of the house. Now the effort is being made not only to lift the ban but for a declaration legalizing the communist party.
The statement is made that this is the only place in the British empire where communism is illegal.. I take issue with that. There is no place where the common law of Britain prevails that communism is not illegal as a subversive doctrine, and the members of the Labour party in the United Kingdom do not seem to have had very much doubt about
that when they were recently called upon to vote upon the proposal that since the dissolution of the Comintern they should admit the Communist party over there into their ranks. The same situation exists in the United States. Even if this were not on the books in the form of a defence of Canada regulation, the party would still be an illegal organization if, as its thesis always contended, and as was printed not more than fifteen months ago by the secretary of the great Civil Liberties League in Toronto, Mr. A. E. Smith, there is no other way, they themselves say, to institute their system than by violence. They say, "Of course the bourgeois, the capitalist class are never going to submit; we can only by violence overthrow them; we cannot get anywhere without it."

I do not want to interfere with the minister's speech, but I should like to ask one question which I think is pertinent. The underlying principle of communism, as I understand it, is the overthrow of government by force. Is there any evidence in the files of the department which would lead the government to believe that that principle has been repudiated by this body?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	There have been
statements from individuals-

Individuals, yes.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: -repudiating it.

But not from the body?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: 'The case of one man comes to my mind-I have not the file here- who answered, when these theses were put to him, well, of course he was prepared to suffer for those ideas.

May I ask the minister a question? I think he should be careful in naming organizations. I think he is mistaken in Mr. Smith's connection with the organization; I do not think it is the Civil Liberties' League. Probably it has some other name.
The communist party have changed the name and the gentleman still continues in office. It is merely a change of names.

The Civil Liberties'
League is a different organization.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I stand corrected.

Is it the National Council of Democratic Rights?

War Appropriation-Justice

Mr. ST. LAURENT: Possibly. That, is the name.

They change their name so often.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am informed that at one time it was the National Council of Democratic Rights, and another time it was the Canadian Tribune Civil Liberties' Bureau of Toronto.

No; I
think the minister is wrong there. I hold in my hand an advertisement under the auspices of the Civil Liberties' Association of Toronto headed, "Help Canada to do justice," and the first signature is the Hon. H. C. Nixon, premier of Ontario. So that I think there is some error. Surely he is not in that bunch.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would not want any mistake over the designation to cause discomfort.

The minister has not
in mind interning the head of these signatories?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The Department of Justice never has in mind interning anyone until facts are brought to its attention that cause the minister to come to the conclusion that such action is necessary for the safety of the state.

The minister has an open mind on him anyway.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: And on all Canadian citizens.
That situation was dealt with. Section 98 of the criminal code was repealed, and those who were in the house at that time will remember that the late lamented>Mr. Woodsworth taunted my predecessor with tendering with one hand what he was taking away with the other by reason of the amendment which at the same time he caused to be inserted in the code as to what amounts by statute to a seditious intention.

Of course, his reason was that a deal had been made for the repeal of section 98. Yes; a deal was made for the repeal of section 98, and the other correlative part which I think the minister is about to read was not a part of that deal. I remember it very well.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: There was in section 98 practically a whole code which I do not think very many could support in its entirety. But what was inserted was section 133:
Without limiting the generality of the meaning of the expression "seditious intention" everyone shall be presumed to have a seditious intention who publishes, or circulates any

writing, printing or document in which it is advocated, or who teaches or advocates, the use, without the authority of law, of force, as a means of accomplishing any governmental change within Canada.
That is the common law doctrine in the United States, and it was on that doctrine that the attorney general of the United States gave his celebrated opinion in the Brydges case, because anyone is deportable if it is shown that at the time he entered the United States he belonged to an organization that advocated the use of force for the overthrow of American institutions.
To get back to something more within the scope of what is sought from this committee at the present time, this is an appropriation of $35,000 to cover the expenses of advisory committees that act under the defence of Canada regulations. The amount expended last year was almost twice that, because soon after I assumed office I came to the conclusion that there would probably be a large number of those interned who, upon examination of their cases, would be released, and I felt that if it were so in general, it was my duty to see that they got their hearings just as expeditiously as possible. I had three committees sitting practically all the time and about a thousand cases were considered. The situation now is that it will be only occasionally that committees will be required to sit and act, and it is for that reason that the amount of the appropriation asked for at the present time is considerably less than what was expended in the past year.
I was forgetting to speak of the special case referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre. The defence of Canada regulations are a part of the law of the Country and are administered in general, as is the criminal law of the country, by the attorneys general of the provinces. There arises frequently a confusion out of the fact that in some provinces the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has contracts with the provincial government to do provincial policing, and whenever there is something with which a member of the force is apparently connected the impression gets abroad that that is something that is being done by the Department of Justice. Most of the time that is quite wrong; it is something in which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is carrying out duties and responsibilities of the attorney general of the province.

And responsible,
under the Minister of Justice, to account to this parliament.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	A member of the
Royal Canadian Mounted Police is responsible to the Minister of Justice if he does some-

War Appropriation-Justice
thing which is not in accord with the contract entered into by the department with the province under the authority granted by this parliament. This parliament has provided under what conditions contracts may be made with a province or with a municipality to make the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police available to that province or that municipality for the ordinary police work in that locality.

What is the situation with respect to the use of the mounted police in the province of Quebec?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	In the province of
Quebec there is no contract, nor do I think there is with any municipality in that province.

Do they
execute any authority in the administration of justice, in the province of Quebec, under the attorney-general's department?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	They do as sworn
police agents, just as we expect the constables who are sworn under provincial or municipal organizations to cooperate in enforcing peace and order. However, I will make special inquiry with respect to the case to which my hon. friend has called my attention. I had heard nothing at all about it and was certainly aware of no instructions from the department to take these proceedings. I cannot say whether there were instructions from the attorney-general or from the mayor or what you will, but I will inquire and find out what is being done. I can assure my hon. friend, however, that there were no instructions from the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in that connection. The hon. member was under a misapprehension when he suggested that, though proceedings might be started by anyone, they could not be continued without the concurrence of the Attorney-General of Canada or the attorney-general of the province. That would be true under regulation 39, but prosecutions under 15 (a), for distributing pamphlets that do not show the printer's name and address, are not subject to that special requirement, and that article can be enforced under the ordinary terms of the summary convictions provisions.

Then the
minister suggests that as far as Quebec is concerned, taking the instance referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre, the attorney-general's department of that province would have no jurisdiction and no right to command the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	No right to command the services of the mounted police, but the factual situation is that the mounted police making investigations in any part of the province report them to the attorney-general of Quebec or his accredited representatives, and sometimes they are asked by the attorney-general or his representatives to make a complaint upon which proceedings are originated. But that is as peace officers and not because they are subject to any direction by the attorney-general.

Full responsibility for their action is still here.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	Full responsibility
for the action of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police acting as such is here.

Or in any capacity, I should think.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would not say in any capacity, because there have been judgments where damages were claimed; for instance, where it was contended that a peace officer did not engage the responsibility of those who appointed him when he was exercising statutory powers given by the criminal code or other like legislation to a peace officer.

We pay them and they should be responsible here.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: They should be responsible for what they are required to do, and as a matter of fact the commissioner holds them responsible to him for whatever they do.

Which means that you hold him responsible to you?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I hold him responsible to me, and I attempt to defend before this house the discipline he enforces among his men.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to hold up these items at all, but seeing there has been no explanation made in connection with the various items, I thought I would make a brief explanation as they are called. In connection with the export permit branch I would inform the committee that at the request of the Department of Munitions and Supply, the wartime prices and trade board and other branches charged with conserving Canada's supplies, a great number of Canadian commodities are placed under permit before they can be exported. This branch considers the application, and either issues or refuses the necessary permit, after consultation with the various administrators and controllers.
Permits are refused for one or more of the following reasons: To conserve materials for Canada's own war effort, or that of the united nations; to conserve supplies for Canadian civilian use; to conserve supplies in order that our commitments to the United Kingdom may be fulfilled; because of dangerous destinations or undesirable consignees.
Will there be an opportunity to discuss the report of the wheat board, or should that discussion come under some other item?
I do not think there is any possibility of discussing wheat under any of these items. I hoped that the civil estimates for my department would be up within a short time.
When is that likely to be?
I cannot promise what may happen in the house, but I hope they will be before us shortly. I shall do my best to have them before the committee as soon as possible.
What were the expenditures last year?

To a great extent this is a new development in the Department of Trade and Commerce. In the past year or two we have been talking over matters connected with the war. Those are the items under consideration to-night, and they are entirely separate and apart from the ordinary estimates of the department.

This is
purely an administration item. How big a staff has the minister? I thought a good deal of this work was being done by permanent officials from other departments?

Yes; there is quite a substantial staff. But a substantial number of them are officers of the Department of Trade and Commerce who have been holding other positions throughout the world as trade commissioners or assistant trade commissioners. These men are in Ottawa, having returned from overrun countries and, as the hon. member has said, they are being used very effectively on this work.
Would the minister deal with permits issued for the export of feed grains to the United States?
The export of feed grains does not come under this item. This item refers to export permits granted to the departments I mentioned.

This is the first opportunity this year we have had of dealing with the Department of Trade and Commerce. As hon. members are aware, these items refer entirely to war appropriations. The war has made a great many changes in the functions of this department. The chief difficulties I see in the work of this department are those which can be traced to the war. We must remember that, so far, trade has always followed the flag. To a great extent our trade has been carried on within the empire, and that portion of it carried on outside the empire has developed extensively through most-favoured nation agreements.
This is the first opportunity the committee has had to discuss our export and import trade, a process upon which the whole empire has developed. We have had many agreements affecting exports and imports. Trade is closely related to other problems of the empire to which we belong, and to the world at large.

War Appropriation-Trade ami Commerce
For instance, defence is closely connected with trade. We have export and import trade. As we know, our development on the seven seas has been built up largely by our trade with the motherland and the empire. We did have an empire agreement with all the dominions and the crown colonies. The Department of Trade, and Commerce has sent its commissioners throughout the world, and as a result we are very closely connected with our best customers.
Our best customer, however, is the mother country. She cannot any longer exist unless she is linked up with the empire. During the war we have seen the result of the disarmament policy, one which nearly finished Great Britain and nearly finished Australia and New Zealand. It also nearly finished the trade of this country.
I suggest that under this war appropriation measure the minister should state what Canada's policy and position is. We should be told our position now, as a result of the war, and as a result of our trade with our best customers. This empire had its being by the sea, and it cannot exist without the sea and the dominions. The senior dominion is Canada. We are still linked up with our best customer, and without that bond I do not think the empire could exist. As hon. members know, we have in Canada an abundance of raw materials.
The minister has done a very good job in expanding Canada's trade. He has developed to a greater extent trade with South America and with other parts of the outside world. We would hope, too, that our trade with those countries might continue after the war. I believe, however, that in connection with the war appropriation estimates the minister should sound a policy which would be well recognized and admitted. As I have pointed out on other occasions, the mother country has to import twenty-five out of twenty-seven of her raw materials. To a great extent she has to depend upon the empire for her supplies of those materials. I believe in the old policy of accepting an exchange of manufactured goods from her for raw materials.
Let us not forget that New Zealand, Australia and all the rest of the empire is linked up in this great fight. They have fought a good fight, and the empire has nearly beaten their enemy from without. The enemy from within, the war losses and depressions and that sort of thing, may still have to be faced. I would point out to the minister that last year Great Britain made a strong and binding agreement with Russia, under which Britain becomes what might almost be called, with Russia, the police constable of trade and commerce on the seas at both ends of Europe.
The dominions are not parties to that treaty. The Anglo-Soviet treaty affects only the United Kingdom. It was signed without committing the other dominions in any way. The influence which Britain will have in the post-war period and in discussing the peace terms will depend largely upon the unity of her dominions. If the dominions try to stand alone as independent countries in trade and for defence purposes, they will not get on because none of them can stand alone without the empire. The dominions and the empire must be a unit in a military way, in a trade way or in a commerce way, because they are absolutely correlated and coordinated. I am one of those who believe that notwithstanding what has been done there will always be nations and international trade. We are largely dependent upon the motherland which has been our best customer in peace and war alike.
The empire must be maintained, I was glad to see the announcement made of an empire , civil air conference-I do not know whether it is official-about the part that civil aviation will play after the war. We nearly lost the lead in civil aviation to the United States. I hope the Department of Trade and Commerce will look into this, because civil aviation is going to be one of the greatest agencies of trade. I hope it will be free from the war ministry. The dominions have had agreements for interimperial trade. We want to trade with South America, but we must not forget that we are part and parcel of the British empire. I am opposed to these ideas of internationalism that would force us to give up the sovereignty rights to our bases. I believe we should conserve our rights in these bases since in trade and commerce under our shipping laws the world's ships can go into any British port to do trade with us, provided these ships obey our port and municipal laws and do not attempt to engage in coastal trade. We should conserve the rights to these bases, and be ready to cooperate with our allies in trade, but no sovereignty over any of them should be given away to any other nation. They are empire ports.
Britain and the dominions have flourished as a result of trade carried on. The British empire has been a great customer of this country and it must continue to be. Great Britain is highly industrialized and we must continue to do business with her and give her liberally of the raw materials she needs. She has been one of our best customers. She must, import twenty-five of the twenty-seven essential raw materials she uses, such as oil, iron, zinc, copper, tin, rubber, cotton, wool and timber. We never realized how important
4868	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
were our relations with the mother country until the far east was lost. As individual members of the empire we can do nothing, but collectively we have a great advantage. The British colonies under the colonial policy of the mother country have provided raw materials for the whole world without let or hindrance or interference. Notwithstanding the fact that the colonies in the West Indies and the far east had trade agreements with the mother country, nothing was done to prevent them from supplying raw materials freely to the rest of the civilized world. We must do everything to help our empire trade because we cannot get on without it.
We should be ready to cooperate with our allies and allow them to use these air bases, but we should not give away sovereignty over them. The empire has thrown back its enemies from without and in my opinion she will go on to destroy them. Now is the time that we should try to recapture the spirit of empire and our faith and pride in our dominions and in our trade and commerce. The empire is a living thing and should not be allowed to go by default or into liquidation. The mother country and the dominions fought this battle alone for two years. Our soldiers carried on with those from India, New Zealand, South Africa, Australia and the empire training plan. We stood shoulder to shoulder in the snows of Labrador and Newfoundland and in the heat of India and the far east.
In the days before the war you could go into any large port and find fifteen or sixteen ships from different parts of the empire carrying on their trade. I believe that this same spirit of empire cooperation will continue in the years that are to come. Canada should be ready to go along with the dominions and the empire. The time has come when the Minister of Trade and Commerce should tell this committee and the country what our relations are with the other sister dominions who fought along with us for two years to save civilization. One of our great allies stood aside for two years with Germany, but Russia has since made a glorious record. To-day she is practically fighting her battles alone except for some supplies and munitions that are being sent in. Poland fought her battle alone, but now the dominions are united together in this fight in North Africa and in other parts of the world. Now is the time to build up our empire trade. The empire is our best customer. It stood by us when we were a small dominion. I should like to conclude by quoting what has been said in a great textbook by

Professor Macneile Dixon, a great Scotsman, who has been interested in our empire and our trade. He said:
Civilizations arise, and continue to exist- and all history is witness to the truth-when conditions are hard, only when they are continually threatened, only when they are determined to maintain and defend their rule. They decline and fall when the external pressure is removed, or the inner spirit . . . decays. If an individual or a people ceases to believe in itself, its aims and ideals, others with firm aims and beliefs will climb into the saddle. The decline and fall of England, which will rejoice our enemies, will not be England's decline and fall only, but of all for which she stood, and not till then shall we know the extent of our miseries. I, at least, am not of the opinion that humanity, justice, freedom, no, nor Christianity, will be the gainers in that fall.
Up to now our sister dominions have borne the brunt of the war, and we should rejoice to have attained the success we have recently in driving back the enemy. We should also rejoice to get into a close partnership with the other dominions and with the mother country with a view to making a better world.
I do not believe altogether in all this international policy. If we had had an international policy which meant the giving up of empire ports like Gibraltar and Suez, the Cape, the far east and the West Indies, where would we be to-day? The empire would have been destroyed, and that would have meant the fall of civilization. Let us cooperate in matters of trade along the lines of the old shipping laws, allowing other countries to use our ports, but as to giving up our sovereignty -no.
Is this the item under which export permits are granted for shipments of coarse grains?

No. I did not want to interrupt the hon. member for Broadview, but his remarks would have been quite proper on the ordinary estimates of my department. I do not think they were quite appropriate on this particular item. I do not mention that in criticism of him but just as a suggestion to other hon. members.

I desire to deal with the question of the export of lumber, which is a matter of great importance, particularly to western Canada, where a number of small mills had from the beginning of the war contracts for the shipment of lumber to the United States to be used in various defence projects. The contracts allowed for a price to the Canadian producer that assured him of his costs and a profit. But some time ago, I think it was in October last, an order

War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
was made forbidding the export of lumber to the United States, and an order in council was passed by the terms of which relief was given to the Canadian producer from the consequences of his being thus prevented1 from carrying out his contract in the United States.
I should like to have a statement from the minister as to the policy being followed with reference to the export of lumber. That is a subject which is causing a lot of ill feeling in the United States to-day. They feel that they should have the privilege of receiving at least a portion of the lumber that is being produced in western Canada in order to permit of the completion of their defence projects, which are of direct benefit to the united nations. I should like also to know from the minister whether it is the intention of the department or of the board charged with the responsibility of setting the price to set the price at a higher level so as to ensure to the Canadian producers a reasonable profit. On the basis of present prices it is almost impossible for the small producer to get out the lumber at a profit, having regard to his production costs for labour and the like, which have materially increased within the last year.

The hon. member for Lake Centre refers to a situation with which I am familiar through the department and because I know of the difficulties of the lumber producers, particularly in the northern portions of the three western provinces. The matter has had to be decided on the basis of where is the greatest need for lumber. We reached the point where lumber exports to the United States had to be stopped on account of the need for lumber at home in our own war construction projects, not only in western Canada but in all parts of Canada. I do not think there is any misunderstanding in the United States over our action in this matter. We have had conversations with United States authorities, and they are fully aware of our peculiar position and of our requirements for more lumber than we can produce. I am sure the hon. member knows that arrangements have been made to assist the lumber producers at least in part, in compensation for the loss of the higher prices in the United States market.
What is being done?
A bonus is being paid to the producer.
What is the amount?
I am not sure at the moment.
Does this bonus operate through the minister's department?
No; it is paid through the Department of Munitions and Supply.
What percentage of our lumber is being exported to the United States, and what percentage is being retained in Canada?
My understanding is that practically all our lumber is being retained. For a while we allowed lumber to be exported to the United States for purely war purposes. '

The point I am endeavouring to make is this. Our producers in the northern parts of western Canada got out a great deal of lumber in the expectation of receiving a certain price under contracts which they had in the United States at that time. Now they are required to deliver that lumber to Canadian consumers in Canada at a considerably lower price than they were receiving on these United States contracts. The result is that many of our small operators are losing money on the sale of their lumber at the Canadian price, even taking into account the bonus that is given.
I have another question to ask the minister. Exceptions are made from time to time. I am not going to name the company unless the minister asks me to do so, but exceptions have been made. There is an exception made in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, where one large producer is permitted to export to the United States. I should like the minister to explain the basis upon which one company is given an export permit, while another company in the same position is denied the privilege of exporting to the United States and is required to sell to the Canadian market at a lower price.

So far as my department is concerned I do not think that situation exists. I am familiar with the situation my hon. friend describes. I know that the producers to whom he refers in the northern parts of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba were enjoying a lucrative market in the United States. But Canadian needs made it imperative that we stop these shipments to the United States. Recompense has been made in part to these producers, and their loss in part is consequent to the war and is accepted as such.

That still does not answer the question as to the basis upon which consideration is given to one company
4870	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
to make exports from Canada that is denied to others. I know the minister is very much interested in this problem because it is one which affects him, as it affects all members from western Canada. It has caused a great deal of difficulty in these areas of northern Saskatchewan I speak of now, where the export market made possible the production of a great deal of lumber on the basis of the prices which were contracted for. There is a great deal of lumber available in northern Saskatchewan-the same applies in Alberta and Manitoba-which could be got out if only the price were fixed at a level considerably higher than the present price.
Labour is the real difficulty.

These lumber producers had certain definite commitments in the United States. The contracts permitted them to pay higher wages than otherwise would have been the case. Last fall the situation in Saskatchewan was this, that many of these smaller lumber producers were ordered to ship their lumber to wholesalers in Saskatchewan and Manitoba at a price considerably lower than the prices which the producers had contracted for in the United States. But the benefit did not pass to the consumer. The producers had a certain fixed price designated by the Department of Munitions and Supply, I assume, in cooperation with the Department of Trade and Commerce. They were directed to deliver lumber at such price to wholesalers in the western provinces, and the wholesaler in turn took that lumber, at a price of 834 including the freight, or of around $28 or $30 at the place of shipment, but the price paid by the consumer, the farmer who required lumber to build granaries and the like, was considerably in advance uf the price which was paid by the wholesaler.
My suggestion is this, that in order to induce and accelerate production of lumber, the producer should be allowed to sell to his own customers instead of being directed to sell through the medium of other wholesale concerns. In that way the producer would be induced by the extra price to produce more lumber than he is producing to-day, would be able to secure a fair profit, and the consumer would be assured of receiving lumber at a price considerably lower than now prevailing. I realize that there was a necessity for putting into effect an embargo against the shipment of lumber outside Canada by reason of needs within Canada, but I submit that in making that determination of policy the government

should have set a price so that the producer would be assured of a fair and reasonable profit, which is not the case to-day, I make a plea to the minister that consideration be given to increasing the price by increasing the bonus. There is any amount of lumber available; all that is required is a price which will assure the small producer of a profit, and I think the needs of western Canada, particularly for granaries for the crops this fall and for necessary defence projects, will be secured. But to follow the present policy will mean an ever-increasing shortage of lumber production, which is something we want to guard against at this time.
I should like the minister to explain the basis upon which the board determines that certain companies shall have the privilege of exporting whereas on the other hand others are denied that right.

I
am not sure that the hon. member understands that the Department of Trade and Commerce in its handling of export permits is the machinery through which those permits are issued or refused. We handle them at the request of various other departments of government. Most of the hon. gentleman's argument is based, I think, on the reasons those departments have for asking us to put the export permit against those products. At the same time I have been in very close touch with the operation of this, and I would be greatly interested in hearing that any individual lumber producer in any of the western provinces or elsewhere in Canada has a preferred position in relation to any other. I shall be very glad to make inquiries of the department having to do with that.
I do not want to get into any long argument upon this, but I think the hon. gentleman was more or less advocating that there should be higher prices paid for lumber so that a higher wage scale could be paid.
He did not say that.
No-so that a profit will be returned to the producer which will accelerate production.
And compensate him for the lost contracts.

As I have said, compensation is paid to a certain extent. I am quite aware of the fact stated by the hon. member for Lake Centre that the lumber producers are not satisfied with the bonus which has been given to them. I have heard from too many of them to have any

War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
doubt about that. But I also am under the impression, and I am quite satisfied I am correct, that these producers can sell direct to retailers.

How large
is the bonus paid?
It is not in my department, and I have not the figures under my hand.
I think the item should stand until the minister gets the information.

But this is an administrative item, and therefore every phase of the position is capable of being discussed under this item. If a bonus is being paid under this export system, information of the amount should be available under this item.
I just want to reiterate what I have said: it is not a matter of this department at all, it is a matter of another department for which we are handling export permits.

I do not wish to be misunderstood as saying that they do not have the right to sell to consumers, but they have not the available methods of distribution, having no yards, and therefore are required by order to deliver to the distributing agencies.
They can start a yard if they like.

Yes. They could
start a yard if they liked; that is true enough. Lumber companies in Ontario are allowed to export to the United States to-day, are they not? They have that right even at the present time, provided the lumber is going to users who are working on direct war orders. Why, then in view of the fact that Ontario producers of lumber have that right, have western Canadian producers of lumber not the same right? There is one lumber company in the province of Manitoba that has the right to export fire-killed lumber to the United States. I should like the minister to look into this matter. It is one that vitally affects many small operators in the northern parts of the three
western provinces. They ask why it is that they are denied the privilege, which to-day is extended to operators in the province of Ontario, of shipment to the United States.

May I reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Marshall). As far as my department is concerned, this branch carries itself. The total expenditure of the branch to March 31, 1943, was 899,842.11, and the total revenues for the same period were $139,727.53.

The minister stated
that the payment of the bonus on shipments of lumber to the United States was not a matter which concerned his department. Would this be the direct concern of the wartime prices and trade board operating under the Department of Finance?
I believe the particular question under discussion has been a matter for munitions and supply.

Item agreed to.
Canadian shipping board-
Adminisration, $92,435.
Revolving chartering fund, $500,000.
Total, $592,435.

Is this a
new item?
