This requires a substantial explanation.

The responsibility and functions of this board are to advise the government, or government departments concerned, on matters relating to war-time shipping; to ensure that the Canadian merchant marine is used to maximum efficiency in the war effort; to service and to control the movement of Canadian waterborne trade; and to administer its own regulations governing Canadian vessels; to work in cooperation with the United Kingdom ministry of transport and the United States war shipping administration; to ensure that neutral shipping shall operate as far as possible in the interests of the united nations. There is a revolving chartering fund in connection with the operations. The purpose of the vote is to provide a fund upon which the Canadian shipping board can draw for necessary war-time chartering operations in the national interest. The money is not actually expended but only loaned. It is returned to the government by payments for space et cetera.

War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce

What is
the set-up of the board which is to have this $500,000? Who is the head of the board? The minister's statement is a very general one dealing with principle; there are no details in it at all. What is the name of the board?
The Canadian shipping board.
Who is the head of it?
Mr. MacCallum. He is an able and experienced man on loan from one of the shipping companies.

Does this board cooperate with the Park Steamship company who are chartering out to merchants or traders ships built by the Canadian government, and likewise loaning ships to Great Britain and operating, besides, twelve or fourteen ships for the Canadian government?
This board handles the vessels to which the hon. member refers. Some of them are operated by the Park Steamship company and some by other agencies.
Do they control shipping on the great lakes?
Has this board anything to do with inland shipping on the great lakes?
Yes.

Will the minister give some idea of the situation with regard to the boats necessary for the movement of grain on the great lakes? At present there is a considerable demand for coarse grains in the United States, but apparently there is lack of shipping space. The other day the Minister of Agriculture stated in the house that there was a tremendous shortage of railroad cars for the movement of grain, and I was surprised at what I read in the evidence given before the special committee on reconstruction and reestablishment, on July 8, by Mr. Vaughan, chairman and president of the Canadian National Railways. In answer to a question with reference to this point he stated:
We can handle a lot more grain than is being offered. There was a time at the first when we were rather short of cars; but Mr. Walton attended several meetings on that and I think he can give you more information than I.
Mr. Walton then made this statement:
We attended the meetings of the grain committee of the cabinet and other meetings. The situation is this, that during the severe winter weather handlings were naturally cut down.

Ever since the cessation of bad weather we have been in a position to handle a considerably greater quantity of grain than has been rolling. Various causes contributed to it but as far as the railway position is concerned we can handle more than is being offered to us at the moment -I am speaking only for the Canadian National, of course.
Later on, Mr. Walton made this further statement:
But again there was a marked increase in the rail movement of feed grain to eastern Canada, of which we can handle any reasonable quantity they offer us.
We all know that the price of these grains in the United States is much above the Canadian price, and as a result of that a considerable premium is paid in the form of an equalization fee on these grains being shipped to the United States. In the Rural Cooperator of Tuesday, July 13, this statement appeared:
To-day the government is asking 34 cents per bushel for export permits on barley going to the United States, and 17 cents per bushel on oats. . . .
In view of the price the western farmer has been receiving for his coarse grain, below cost of production, the government should make every effort to see that this grain is moved at this time so that the premium may be obtained. The railway companies state that they have cars. Will the minister explain what the situation is on the great lakes as regards the movement of this grain? I am referring not only to the movement of grain to the United States, because large quantities of grain should be brought to eastern Canada for consumption this winter. There will be a scarcity of these grains, and if we have a severe winter, as we had last year, the railroads may find themselves unable to handle the grain. The shipping situation on the great lakes is of vital importance to the west. Apparently there is a shortage of bottoms. What are they being used for? Exactly what is the situation?

The boats on the great lakes which in pre-war days handled wheat more or less exclusively to-day are handling munitions and war supplies, principally ore which they take to eastern points. The situation is being given careful attention by the people who are interested in moving coarse grains and wheat from the west to the east. Some time ago I saw statements which were made by the railway companies before one of the committees of this house to the effect that more grain could be carried by them, intimating they had cars available to carry more grain from western Canada. I immediately took up this matter with the wheat board in Winnipeg, who replied' expressing

War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
their surprise that such statements should be made, since that was not their understanding, and as a matter of fact according to their information the car shortage remained1 very acute. I wrote to at least one of the railways, pointing out these facts and referring to the statement that had been made before the committee here, and I asked for an explanation.
I believe that letter went out only yesterday, and as yet there has not been time for a reply. The hon. member knows western Canada, and I am sure he realizes that there is a very great shortage of box cars there. At the present moment I believe there are, between the head of the lakes and western Canada, cars loaded with thirty million bushels of wheat. There has been delay in unloading those cars on account of an acute labour situation at the head of the lakes. Through the Department of Labour and other departments of government we have brought all possible pressure to bear on the situation, in an effort to take care of that bottleneck. Everyone recognizes the seriousness of it; everything possible is being done, yet we are not meeting with very' great success.

I wanted to ask a question with regard to shipping on the great lakes and the control of the United States vessels engaged in that trade. I also wanted to know if this board had control over the rates charged, but when I asked whether this shipping board had any jurisdiction over lake shipping the minister said, no.
I did not understand the question.

The minister said the shipping board had nothing to do with that matter, but then he allowed the hon. member for Melfort to bring it up again. So that I think he was just a little hasty in replying to me.
I am very sorry; I just did not understand the hon. gentleman's question.
Then would the minister tell us how many United States boats are taking wheat from Fort William at the present time?
I cannot give that information.
Has there been any increase in lake rates on grain carried by United States vessels from Fort William to United States ports, since the opening of navigation?
I cannot give that information, either. I believe all these questions could be answered when my own estimates are brought down.
The Minister has not the information before him?
No.

I understand that this board must either approve or disapprove when one of the defence departments desires to acquire a vessel; that is, the Canadian shipping board is asked to consent or otherwise when a vessel is chartered or acquired by one of the defence departments. It seems to me the board can be of great service in guarding the interests of the ship owners on the Atlantic coast, in particular, if it performs its duties as it should. I would suggest that before a vessel is either purchased or chartered, this board should go into the question very carefully, to see whether or not a boat cannot be built for the purpose, or obtained from some other source, so that commerce and trade will be disrupted as little as possible. We find that a boat may be acquired from an individual who has no other means of earning a livelihood. I urge the minister to make representations to the board so that careful attention may be given to these matters, with a view to causing as little disturbance as possible when boats are required by the defence departments.
I shall be glad to do that.

The minister said that thirty million bushels of grain were loaded in cars because it was impossible to get labour to unload them. To me that is a serious matter, just when we are approaching another harvest; certainly it is going to be a tremendous worry to many western producers. I wonder if the minister would say what space is available for grain in the terminals, provided it can be unloaded from the cars. He might tell us also how long those cars have been loaded, either at Fort William or in transit. I think that would be useful information for the producers, who would like to know what they will be up against during harvest time.

I am speaking from memory, but I think at the present time there is space for something like sixty to seventy million bushels. Within the last twenty-four hours permission has been secured from the proper authorities to increase the pay of the men who are doing this difficult and dirty job at the head of the lakes. Then we thought we might be able to get some
4874	COMMONS
War Appropriation*-Trade and Commerce
surplus labour from internal elevators throughout western Canada, and that position has been explored very thoroughly. As I stated, we have been in close contact with labour, asking for a high priority; we have had these units classed as war units, and have been doing everything possible to get the necessary labour. I quite realize that the situation is serious, as the hon. member for Souris has said, with another crop coming along in western Canada. I might add that only today I had further assurances, though they were not too definite, that the officials are hopeful that the whole quota can still be taken before the end of the crop year.

I shoud like to ask the minister a question in regard to these permits. The minister has said that the issuing of permits does not Come under his department, but as the hon. member for Melfort has suggested, the export of feed grain does come more or less under this department, and it seems to me we have two serious situations in Canada, both of which are aggravated by the shortage of shipping. We have an abundance of grain out west, which I am led to believe has been stored in the fields, while in Ontario and eastern Canada we have empty granaries, and the prospects are that there will be a crop only in Ontario. The farmers of this province have increased their live stock since the beginning of the war, and it is essential that a good deal of that grain be moved east. I know that will be a tremendous job, with the serious car shortage, but I feel that some effort must be made to work out a scheme under which the farmer in Ontario with the empty granary will be able to relieve the western farmer of his abundance which he cannot store. It seems to me essential that some shipping space be made available, or else both the farmer in the west with the surplus of grain and the farmer in the east with the abundance of live stock and an empty granary are going to lose. I do not think we can lightly pass over this problem;
I believe we must so direct our efforts and energy that we can relieve both these serious situations, or in other words kill two birds with one stone.
I should like to have something fairly definite on this, because I live in a live stock district, and I have received many inquiries from farmers who are very much worried over the prospect of this grain not coming to Ontario, in view of the fact that there is such a demand in the United States at a higher price. It is true that the farmers of eastern Canada are protected by the ceiling price. I noticed that the hon. member for Melfort quoted from the Rural Cooperator.
I brought along a copy of the same paper, 
from which I intended to read; then the hon. member went on to say that he was anxious to see the government make haste in order that the western farmer might get the benefit of the premium which is being offered. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that the eastern farmers are just as. anxious to get some benefit from that premium, too, because if that grain is to be brought here and fed to live stock, it is necessary that the eastern farmer be able to purchase it as cheaply as possible. We are prepared to share the benefit with the western farmer, but we do not want him to have all the benefit. I think some way should be worked out under which this benefit could be shared equally as between east and west.

I was not saying anything against the eastern farmer getting the grain. As a matter of fact I was anxious that he should get it, and that is why I was asking that the shipping situation be investigated and more boats made available. Certainly it is a serious situation when twenty thousand of our railroad cars should be tied up because they cannot be unloaded. That is what it means, if we have thirty million bushels of grain in transit; twenty thousand railroad cars are tied up, storing grain, when they should be moving the grain to the head of the lakes. If it is the labour situation, selective service should certainly get some of these men who are at present working in non-essential industries, and put them where they would be doing something useful for the war effort. We have a labour department and a selective service organization in the dominion to attend to people engaged in non-essential industries, and it is time selective service got to work and used a little bit of compulsion to see that necessary things are done first.

I should
like to have a little more information with respect to this new departure of establishing a revolving fund of $500,000 for this Canadian shipping board. I assume that this is working capital for the board. Why is it necessary that government funds should be put up for this purpose? I venture to suggest it is the first time the government of the day has supplied working capital for chartering ships and carriers by water for domestic and foreign transportation. We know that all ocean transportation is under the control of the British ministry of shipping, so that of necessity the operations of this board must be confined to the domestic situation. I find it difficult to understand, although there may be good reason, the necessity for this new departure. Have we to charter United States bottoms to carry our goods on the great lakes, and is it

War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
a government movement that is being. carried in those vessels? If that were so, I could understand there would have to be a certain amount of working capital advanced through this department, or some other agency, to take care of that position. However, the minister did not make clear what the position was, and since this is a new vote involving a substantial sum I believe we ought to have some further explanation.
I wish to make sure that this evidence of working capital will come back to the treasury. That, to my mind, is important. If this is a business proposition, I would be in favour of it; but I should like to know something more about it.

As I said, the money is used as a fund from which to draw when chartering vessels. At times when a vessel is chartered certain advances have to be made. That money is recovered by the carrying charge on the freight.

Out of
the freight?
Yes.

The minister has been
talking about elevator space. Would he tell the committee what space is available in government terminal and other public terminal elevators, east of the great lakes? For instance, I am informed within the last week that the terminal at Prescott is practically empty. Why should that be?

I
think we are getting pretty far afield. However, in answer to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle I would explain that I have been checking up recently on spare capacity or space in elevators in the east, and I am informed that whereas there has been a certain amount of space available recently, it is expected that this will be used very shortly, through the operations of the wheat board.

Item agreed to.
Shipping priorities committee-
Administration, $59,960.
Gift of wheat to Greece, $6,000,000.

Would
the minister explain these items?

The work of this committee is to ensure that shipping supplies will be made available for essential war supplies, and that non-essential supplies will not take all available shipping space. This committee cooperates closely
with the controllers and administrators, and its work dovetails with the work of the Canadian shipping board.
This is a new agency, is it?
Yes.
Are these civil servants, or are they new men brought in to do the work?
Trade commissioners are in charge.
This is being charged as a war appropriation, and not to civil estimates. Will there be a corresponding reduction in the civil estimates of the department?
Yes; that is correct.

This item includes the
shipment of wheat to Greece. I understand the minister was at an eastern terminal recently celebrating the loading of a vessel. Would he inform the committee

*
Are we considering that item?
I understood the Chairman to read it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I called the two together because, generally speaking, the lengthy discussion takes place on the administration item, and the shipment to Greece is rather, closely connected.
Out of what crop year was the wheat taken? Was it from the 1940, 1941 or 1942 crop?

I
am sorry I have not that information. Here again I do not wish to become involved in the discussion of a matter which might more properly be discussed at another time. However, I imagine the wheat board took it on the basis upon which they have been delivering grain, namely a percentage from one year, a percentage from another, and a percentage from another. As the hon. member knows, wheat is wheat, and a particular crop cannot be identified except as to quantity.

If some of the 1939 or
prior crops, of which they have quite a surplus, were taken at the price indicated, it would make quite a difference. There would be a considerable difference if it were taken at last year's price.
4876	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Trade and Commerce
Mr. MaeKINNON (Edmonton West): I believe it is well known that this gift of wheat has been made to relieve suffering and privation caused by the German invasion of Greece.

We understand that.
Mr. MaeKINNON (Edmonton West): It is a free gift of 550,000 bushels of wheat per month to the people of Greece. To date these shipments total well over 5,000,000 bushels.

What will the total bushel-age be for the $6,000,000?
Mr. MaeKINNON (Edmonton West): We are continuing to give Greece this quantity of wheat per month.
Is the board taking up any of the options at this price in the open market?

What return will a wheat grower get from this $6,000,000 worth of wheat being sent to Greece?
Mr. MaeKINNON (Edmonton West): The hon. member means those who have an interest in participation certificates.

The actual grower of the wheat.
Mr. MaeKINNON (Edmonton West): He will get the market price.

Will he get the market price, or will he get the price which is allotted to the particular year, depending upon what wheat is shipped1? Are futures bought and filled out of this year's crop? What is the position?
Mr. MaeKINNON (Edmonton West): This is a gift of wheat.

We all
know that. The minister does not need to tell us that again.
Mr. MaeKINNON (Edmonton West): I am not in position to say from which crop this wheat will come, nor am I in position to say what price is agreed upon, but I have no doubt it is the proper price.
Of course that is not good enough.

When the wheat board officials were here they told us that in making shipments out of the country they took wheat from different years. They did not want to take it from one year because, if it were sold at a good price, that year would make a profit, but if it were sold at a loss, that year would make a loss. Therefore, in selling any

quantity of wheat they would allocate a certain amount to each year, so that each year will be suffering together or making a profit. I presume in making the shipment of S6,000,000 worth of wheat to Greece they will allocate a certain portion to each year and charge it up to the government accordingly.

Is that the position? I should like to have my information from the minister, and I say that with all respect for the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) who probably knows more about it than the minister.
Mr. MaeKINNON (Edmonton West): Quite possibly.
He is doing pretty well.

The minister is not doing prettty well at all. The minister just knows that this is a gift of $6,000,000 worth of wheat; but where it comes from or where it goes to or from what crop it comes from or what price is being paid, the minister does not know any more about it than I do. I make that statement and I think I am pretty near within the mark.

I do not think the question has been properly answered. While what the hon. member for Wood Mountain has said is the fact to some degree, the practice is to average the sales from the years from which the wheat is taken, and until settlement is made no one can say what the price will be.

Is this not a gift of wheat which will be shipped within the next twelve months?
Mr. MaeKINNON (Edmonton West): This sum is to purchase wheat that will be shipped.

Is it intended to limit the amount of wheat to be shipped to Greece to $6,000,000 worth or will the government continue to ship as long as there is a need and shipping space is available?
Mr. MaeKINNON (Edmonton West): As long as shipping space is available and as long as we have the wheat to give, we will send 26,000 tons to Greece every month.

Item agreed to.
Shipping priorities committee-.
Steamship subsidies war stabilization fund, $500,000.
Mr. MaeKINNON (Edmonton West): It has been necessary to grant increased subsidies to various steamship companies in﻿JULY 15, 1943	4877
War Appropriation-Research Council
order to enable them to carry on under wartime conditions. Additional bonuses are paid in the operation of such services, namely, first, to provide for war bonuses to crews of vessels; second, war risk insurance on the vessels; and third, increased expenditures on fuel, marine insurance, et cetera. People who have contracts with the department which are expiring are coming to us with their audited statements to show that they cannot possibly carry on with their present contracts. This fund enables us to pay, after investigation, increased bonuses for the continuation of services where necessary.
It is just another bonus on account of the high cost of living and operation. Who is to get this $500,000?
There will be different amounts to different people.

I suppose there will be; I do not suppose that one man will get it all, but the minister must have details in front of him of the various ship companies, local and otherwise, which will get this $500,000. We should like to know how it is to be allocated.
I shall have that information available on my ordinary estimate.
The minister does not have it now?
I have not.

The point is that this half million dollars is being taken out of the war appropriation instead of the civil estimates in order to carry on civil operations, the increased cost of which is on account of the war. Is that the right explanation?
That is right.

Item agreed to.
National research council-
Special war activities, $2,114,708.

The reason for this item appearing in the war appropriation is obvious. There have been increased investigations on account of the war, and this vote is to permit the national research council to carry on investigations into war problems and to permit the expansion of investigations into certain problems which are now in progress. There is an item under
national research council in my ordinary estimates. I have been asked by many people, both inside and outside the house, for a more or less detailed report on the work of the national research council. That is a report which it is difficult for a layman to give; that is a report in the preparation of which great care must be taken because of the many war investigations and experiments that are being carried on by the national research council. Anticipating that there would be a great deal of information that hon. members would like to have, I have had a statement carefully prepared covering the operations of the council and it is my intention to ask the consent of the committee to place this on Hansard so that hon. members may have an opportunity to read and study it. Questions can be submitted when my ordinary estimates are up for consideration.
Is it very long?
Yes, it is.

I have asked for certain returns in this connection, and there is one in particular to which I should like to have an answer. This was in connection with the manufacture of synthetic rubber. I have never been able to obtain the exact comparison between the cost of using wheat alcohol and a petroleum base in the manufacture of synthetic rubber. If this information could be obtained, I think it would be most beneficial. A recent article was put out by the line elevators stating that this could be cut in half.

I believe the information the hon. member for Souris is anxious to get will be found in what I am asking to be placed on Hansard. If it is not, the hon. member can tell me within the next day or so, and I shall be glad to see that it is prepared for him.

Is there
anything in the report with respect to alcohol produced from potatoes, which is a live question in my part of the country? You cannot have it all wheat and petroleum.
I think the hon. member will find a comparison of figures in the report.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Then by unanimous leave of the committee shall the report be inserted in Hansard. Is that the pleasure of the committee? Carried.

The report is as follows:

War Appropriation-Research Council
NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL Industrial Uses of Wheat
The possibility of using wheat for the production of war chemicals is a question which has often been raised and is a problem which has received a great deal of consideration. Alcohol has been produced from starchy materials for a very long time and the processes involved are well known. Production methods have been developed to the point where increased yields of alcohol per bushel of grain cannot be expected. However, improvement in manufacturing technique might slightly reduce conversion costs. Wheat yields alcohol in proportion to the amount of starch present, and in most Canadian varieties the maximum possible yield is in the neighbourhood of 2 gallons per bushel. Since the conversion cost is from 15 to 17 cents per gallon, it is evident that the total cost of producing alcohol from wheat is chiefly dependent on the initial price of the wheat. Therefore when wheat sells for 90 cents per bushel, the manufacturing cost of alcohol would not be less than
90 = 45 cents + 17 cents = 62c per gallon.

Item agreed to.

War Appropriation-Post Office
The understanding is that all these matters may be reverted to when the minister's civil estimates come up, because we really require more information.
So far as civil matters are concerned, but I do not think the hon. member would wish to discuss again purely war items.

I should
like to have a break-down of some of these items. However, I know what will be done. About Friday or Saturday of next week, when everybody wants to get home, items will be railroaded through at the rate of a million a minute.
I hope we are through before that.

Perhaps
I am not optimistic enough. But I say that that practice is not good enough when we are dealing with expenditures taken from a tax-ridden people.
Canadian postal corps, $183,020.

I wish to ask a question in
regard to the men in uniform who comprise the Canadian postal corps. I have not all the details, but perhaps the minister would set the matter straight. I understand that a number of the corps are married men living in Ottawa and that they are compelled to live in tents at Lansdowne park. That does not seem like common sense to me because it requires a lot of extra help at Lansdowne park which might be put to some other useful purpose.

This item amounting to $183,020
is made up as follows: temporary assistance, $8,280; cost-of-living bonus, $1,440; travelling expenses, $2,000; printing and stationery, $50,000; equipment and maintenance, $20,000; telegrams and telephones, $600; sundries, $100; mailbags for overseas mail, $100,000; contributions to unemployment insurance fund, $600. There is a decrease from last year of $11,720 in the salaries of these temporary employees. That is due to the fact that the field post offices have now all been placed on an active service basis, and it is therefore no longer necessary to provide an amount for temporary assistance.
The men in uniform in the postal corps to whom the hon. member for Battle River referred are part of the armed services of
Canada and have to carry out the orders given to them by the Department of National Defence just as men in any other branch of the armed services have to do.

Are we
to understand that they were civilians and have been transferred to national defence?

When the corps was set up it was necessary to open post offices in a hurry to give mail service to the troops in the camps, and we had to assign civilians from the different post offices throughout the country to get the service started. But now recruits have been trained in postal work and have joined the postal corps. They are active service men and have replaced the civilians.

They are
charged to the Post Office Department and paid out of the war appropriation?
Yes; the civilians.
Do some of these employees look after the mail in the internment camps?

This is the army postal
service. When we started to set up the service men had to be trained in the work. In the meantime we had to provide a postal service for the different camps, and so we took civilian personnel from the different post offices across the country and put them in to get the service started. They proceeded to train men who had enlisted.

Men of
a lower physical category than Al?
Yes.
Am I right in assuming that the Postmaster General has no control whatever over the men in uniform in the postal corps?
Only so far as directing and looking after the distribution of mail is concerned. In every other respect, discipline, rationing and so forth, they are under the national defence department.
The Post Office Department superintends their activities qua the post office.

Who is the officer in
charge?
Colonel E. J. Underwood. He is at present in England.

Who is in charge of the postal corps in the dominion? Somebody must be in charge in his absence.

War Appropriation-Post Office

Colonel Underwood was sent over to carry out certain duties. Preparations were made well in advance. He is in charge of the personnel of the corps whether they are stationed in England, Canada, North Africa or anywhere else. The man who is permanently in charge of the postal corps in England is Lieutenant-Colonel Ross.
And in Canada?
Colonel Underwood.
Who is in charge when he is away in England?
That is what I was trying to get. Who carries out his duties in his absence?
Captain Warwick.
Is the minister prepared to make any statement as to the better handling of mail for overseas?
Yes.

I think the hon. member
will realize the nature of our transportation difficulty. Our space is allotted to us. We cannot say we are going to occupy so many cubic feet on board a ship or that we are going to put on board so many thousand bags of mail. Space is made available to us and we have to take the space which is allotted and when it is allotted. I think the hon. member will realize what a strain is put upon shipping owing to the African campaign and, now, the operations in Sicily, and that this is bound to slow up the mails at times. But it is purely a question of shipping. We can get the mail to the ports, but we have to wait until there is some ship to put it on. Often we can ship only part of the mail which is available or has been posted on the same day; the rest has to wait until there is space available.

Is this not a correct statement, that for a considerable time -I hope they are not doing it now-the Post Office Department accepted mail to go by air when there were no facilities to convey it by air, and that their so doing really amounted to a deception as far as the senders

of that mail were concerned; they had paid for and consigned it as airmail and the department accepted it as such, though during a considerable period it had not the facilities to convey it by air. That was a justifiable grievance on the part of the senders in this country and of those in the forces overseas.

I agree in part, but not
fully, with what the hon. member has said. He is talking about the thirty cents?

The thirty
cents, and the ten-cent airmail as well.

There was not much of
that. He is wrong in saying that there were no facilities; there were, but not sufficient to take care of the demand. When it was found that the volume could not be handled, notices were sent out and postmasters told to discourage the use of the thirty-cent airmail. We could not tell people that they could not send it that way, because some could go.
The public were not advised, though?
Oh, yes.

The people
who were sending the mail?

Not as individuals, but
they were advised through the press.

Is much of this mail
lost crossing the seas, through the torpedoing of ships?

In the calendar year 1942
we dispatched 14,536 bags of letters, made up of 20,116,360 items, having a weight of 502,909 pounds. The loss owing to enemy action was sixty-five bags of mail.

Very
small.
Those are letters-made up of 2,577 items, sixty-four pounds in weight. Of registered mail sent overseas, 43,687 items were dispatched, and only fifty-six lost.
Fifty-six items?
Fifty-six items. Of news, 40,120 bags were dispatched, and 496 lost through enemy action.
A little over one per cent.

Parcel post, 295,911 bags
dispatched, and 3,187 were lost owing to enemy action. Tobacco parcels, 125,017 bags dispatched, and 3,109 lost.

It is a remarkable
tribute to our naval and air services that such a small amount of mail matter was lost through enemy action.

War Appropriation-Post Office
The department announced some time ago, if I recollect correctly, that a real Canadian airmail service was about to be established. What progress has been made with that?
The service has commenced. The ship has made one westbound trip, but as yet it has not yet completed the round trip.
Just beginning.
Just beginning.

Following the question by the hon. member for Cumberland, I had a return brought down on February 16 along the same line, and it shows that last October thirty per cent of airmail letters went by boat, and thirty-four per cent of the Christmas airmail-ings in December went by boat. I wonder if the minister would be able to state the amount of additional revenue paid by the public on the difference between airmail transported by boat and the ordinary postage rate. I should think it would amount to quite a considerable sum of money.
I know the hon. member will appreciate that at that time of year flying conditions are sometimes very difficult-
I realize that.

-and the planes just cannot go, and airmailings have to wait till the planes can fly. As I stated at the time, a very large accumulation was built up, but it was cleared as quickly as possible. The amount was abnormal and we ran into bad flying weather. The system is greatly improved. But during that time, if I remember correctly, every airgraph message was sent by air; none was sent by surface. I do not think any airgraph message has ever been sent by surface, and perhaps we are the only country in the world which can say that.
Perhaps it was as a result of this that you had the public switch to airgraph. You sent out advices to the public to switch completely to airgraph as a result of this.

We can send so many more messages by airgraph than by any other form of transit. Even the armed forces air letter takes up more space than the airgraph. I might say that we are bringing out a new form, which is airgraph, but which resembles the armed forces air letter. It is on paper so that, if necessary, it can be turned into an airgraph to avoid delays. If it can be handled as 72537-3094
air letter in its ordinary form, it will go that way. I think the hon. member for Souris will understand the importance of that.
Yes.

We might be able to get sufficient transport from here to Great Britain, but from Britain to some other theatre of war we might be able to move it only in small amounts as far as space and weight are concerned, and that we might have to turn letters into airgraphs to get them the rest of the way.
From that point on.

I think we
realize that the minister's department have done the very best they can, and probably under the circumstances they have given splendid service. On the other hand there was a great deal of dissatisfaction and justification for this dissatisfaction. I should like some further information from the minister.
As I understand it, there are three classes of airmail communications; one is the regular thirty-cent airmail letter; another is the ten-cent airmail letter, and the other is the airgraph letter. Would the minister inform the committee for how long a period at any time such letters were held by the Post Office Department for aeroplane service, and in what instances and to what extent such letters were transferred from aeroplanes to be conveyed by ships. There must be some more explanation than the minister has given as to why airgraph and airmail letters, the ten-cent letters, are delayed for at least ten weeks. I should like to know whether in every case such letters went by aeroplane, or were assembled and then went by ordinary mail by steamer.

I am glad the hon. member has brought that up. As I mentioned once before in the house, while we try to do everything we can to expedite mail coming from Great Britain to Canada, we are not responsible; the British government are. We cannot handle that mail until it arrives at a Canadian port.
The hon. member is not talking about that movement.
I am referring to mail from Canadians to overseas forces.

I will give that information. At present, as far as armed forces' air letters are concerned, there is virtually a daily service by air. That is in effect now, subject of course to weather conditions.

War Appropriation-Post Office

I am asking what is the longest period air mail letters were held by the postal department before they were provided with conveyance overseas to our forces and whether such letters were finally conveyed by steamer or by aeroplane.
Is the hon. member referring to the ordinary air letter, the thirty-cent letter, or armed forces letters?
The ten-cent armed forces letters. There was notification with respect to the thirty-cent letter, but there was none with respect to the ten-cent letter.

That is correct. I have not that return. The hon. member for Souris asked for that information and a return was brought down. He referred to that a few moments ago. We gave the amount at that time when he inquired as to what delay there had been in connection with airgraph and armed forces letters, the percentage and so on. It was given then by months and amounts. That information is available on the records.

Will the
minister answer this direct question? In any instance was such mail, after having been held up by the Post Office Department, conveyed by steamer rather than by aeroplane?

Yes; there was a small amount. It is shown in that return. It could not be handled. It would have held up other air letters for a long time on account of the accumulation that had been built up owing to bad flying weather. The planes were not moving in sufficient numbers to handle it, and for days the letters were delayed.
How long were such letters delayed and finally conveyed by aeroplane?
My officials advise me that the longest period was ten days.

I repeat what I have already said. Many people in the armed services did not get their mail for at least ten weeks, and there have also been periods when residents in Canada did not get mail that was sent by those in the armed services in Great Britain for ten weeks or perhaps longer.

As regards the latter part of the hon. member's statement, I have also dealt with that. The Postmaster General of Great Britain advised me of their difficulty and of the accumulation they had on hand. I discussed the whole matter with him last September when I was in England. Their

difficulty was this. A substantial number of planes were going to Britain, but there were not nearly as many coming back this way. Space had to be reserved on the planes to bring back aircrew to ferry more planes back across the Atlantic, and space was not available to the extent that the Postmaster General of Great Britain required.
But that is east to west.
The hon. member mentioned east to west also.

The minister's statement is that there was better service from Canada to Great Britain than from Great Britain to Canada. I should like to get some further information. What service does the department now undertake to give in connection with different classes of air mail: thirty cents, ten cents and airgraph mail? In what time does the department undertake to deliver such communications in Great Britain? I do not say distribute them in Great Britain, but when does it undertake to deliver them in Great Britain, as far as our service is concerned, so that they may be distributed there?
I presume the hon. member is still talking about air.
Yes; the three classes of air mail communications.

As far as airgraph is concerned, weather permitting, it goes daily. It is a comparatively new service. At the beginning, for west-bound airgraphs, we did not have the processing equipment in Canada, and our messages had to be sent to the United States to be processed. They were processed with the American messages in the proportion the number of ours bore to the number of the American messages coming in. If they had a large mail, our processing might be held up for some days, and there was also the additional time of sending it down and getting it back. I am glad to say that now they are processed in Toronto. We managed to get the service performed there, and that has speeded things up considerably, not only for the messages being turned into airgraph on this side but for those processed on receipt from Great Britain or other parts of the world. As regards armed forces air letters, they are going every day subject to weather conditions. As regards the thirty-cent letters, they are going five times monthly.

The minister said a short time ago that an improved service was being put into effect by his department. Is he prepared to give further information in that regard?

War Appropriation-Secretary oj State

Perhaps the hon. member is referring to the statement made by the Minister of Munitions and Supply when he announced the new service being operated by a department of government. We are making use of that.
The postal service uses that?

We use that. At least, we have used it westbound. As a matter of fact, we have brought ordinary mail from the troops back on that. We will speed matters up as far as we can. I cannot say we will handle all mail coming back that way, but we will handle as much as there is space available for.

Is that
Trans-Canada?
Yes, Trans-Canada.

Commission re revocation of naturalization certificates, $5,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I am a
little curious about this item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I think I can explain it.
During the war a great many allegations are made against citizens of Canada who had their origin in enemy countries, to the effect that they are disloyal to the king or disaffected or something else of that kind. Under the Naturalization Act they have the right to have their case heard by a commission before it is acted upon by the Secretary of State. The commissioners under this are Mr. Justice Robson of the court of appeal of Manitoba, Mr. Lee
Kelley of Ottawa and Mr. Aldous Aylen, also of Ottawa. They serve entirely without remuneration. Last year the vote was $10,000; this year it has been cut in half, to $5,000, and the only purpose of the vote is to cover expenses. For example, a great many of these allegations come from various internment camps and other parts of Canada from which the applicant could not possibly come to Ottawa. Consequently, as occasion requires and as the number of cases becomes large enough, the commission visits them at those points and then makes recommendations to the Secretary of State.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
This is
just for travelling expenses, then?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I am
wondering how many naturalization certificates have been revoked, if the minister has that information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Not many under this
provision. There have been quite a few revocations of naturalization papers since the beginning of the war, and one reason for that is that the United States made a complete survey of the citizenship of all its citizens. When it found, for instance, that a person had been naturalized in Canada and had not taken out his papers in the United States, though he might have lived there for quite a number of years, they would notify the naturalization branch to that effect. We would write the person concerned asking if he was prepared to have his naturalization certificate cancelled. I think in all cases it was upon notice, and in the majority of cases they did not even reply. In other cases they said they wished to have their certificates cancelled. I do not think there have been many cancellations of naturalization by this commission, and of course this vote is purely a contingency vote, depending upon the number of applications that are made.

Item agreed to.

Mines and geology branch-to provide for development work to be undertaken by Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada Limited, in connection with tarsands located in the province of Alberta, $150,000.
Will the minister explain the item?
Does this vote cover an amount spent this year, in addition to what was spent last year?

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext: This covers an expenditure that was initiated in the Department of Munitions and Supply, I believe on the recommendation of the oil controller, something over a year ago. Under the arrangements made, an agreement was entered into with the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company to do certain work in connection with drilling, and for the purpose of determining the extent of the tar sands and their quality. It also covered certain expenses in connection with laboratory work carried on to ascertain the best methods of treatment of sands, or the bitumen recovered from the sands. The total amount paid under the agreement up to March 31 last year was $1,234.15. This amount is to reimburse the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company for the expenditures it incurred under that agreement. It will be payable during the current year. That is why the item appears.

I am sorry this work was not undertaken by the tried, trained and experienced men of the Department of Mines and Resources. They were more competent than any other engineers in Canada to do this work of investigating tar sands. They have made investigations along these lines for many years. I repeat that the minister's own engineers were best qualified. They have been doing it, and I am as sure as I am standing here they would have done it for less than the amount mentioned in the item. I cannot understand why outside engineers were sent to do what the minister's own engineers were best qualified to do.

The work was undertaken at cost by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company; that is, they did not plan to make a profit out of it. I suppose one might say it was a contribution from their experience and knowledge.
Of what?

A knowledge which, apparently the hon. member for Davenport questions. At any rate that was the idea when the arrangement was made with the company. May I add that this arrangement was not made by the Department of Mines and Resources, but rather by the Department of Munitions and Supply on the recommendation of the oil controller. The work of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company has terminated.

It is now ended?
4894	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources

In effect, it is terminated. The current work is not being conducted by that company. This estimate is required to pay the company for the work which to a great extent was done last year, but which was not paid for by the end of the fiscal year. It is also for the completion of some tests being made under their supervision.
By whom is the current work being done?

That was all set out in a document tabled in the house some weeks ago. It is being carried out under an agreement between the Department of Mines and Resources and a company known as the Abasand company at Waterways in northern Alberta. The terms of the agreement are set out in the return tabled' in the house. The work will really be under the direction of the Department of Mines and Resources from the time of the agreement, on. The agreement contains provisions not only for the operation of the work, but also for the liquidation of the agreement when it is terminated. If I recall correctly, termination is to be six months after the declaration by the government that a state of war with the enemy has ceased.

I would not want either the minister or the committee to infer from anything I said that I have not the highest opinion of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company, because I have. They are a fine company, and they have splendid engineers. But I was perfectly satisfied with the departmental engineers. They have been in the field for some thirty years and have rendered excellent service. They made a thorough investigation for the department, if the department pamphlets are correct, and I believe they are. I have been over this area on several occasions and I know what the departmental engineers have done. They were competent and did splendid work, and I feel that this work should have been done by the mines and resources department. This is no reflection upon the Consolidated, but I feel that the department should have done this work because their men knew where to go and just what to do. They had the equipment, which the Consolidated did not have when they started. I presume that is why this account is so high. I doubt if the department would have spent 8150,000; they might have spent up to $50,000 or more. It all goes to show that there was not the cooperation there should have been between these two departments of government.

The munitions department sent in outside engineers, and I feel that they should have asked the Department of Mines and Resources to send in their engineers. They were thoroughly qualified; in fact there are none better qualified in North America to carry on tar sand investigations. It is too bad that the munitions department did not ask the Department of Mines and Resources to send its men out there to make inquiry.
Could the minister give us any idea as to how this work is progressing? The agreement has been in effect for several months, and I should like to know what success the company is having.

Before the minister answers, I should like to make one observation. The wording of this item does not correspond with the ministers' statement. He said that this was to cover work that had been done already, but the item reads that it is to provide for development work to be undertaken. The two statements do not quit jibe. Is this a new undertaking, or is it a continuation of a previous undertaking?
The point raised by my hon. friend is quite pertinent, but the facts are as I have stated. The estimate may not be as well worded as it might have been.
We have to take it as it is.

A great deal of expense was incurred last year which this vote is to cover. There are also continuing expenditures to be made for experimental work. The Consolidated Mining and Smelting company arranged for this work with two concerns in the United States, one in Chicago and one in Louisiana.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar wanted some particulars as to how the work is progressing. This agreement was entered into a few months ago-I have not the precise date-with the Abasand company which was operating in the Waterways area. Abasand had been conducting operations largely of an experimental nature for some years past, but as their work progressed they found that changes were necessary in their plant and equipment. An arrangement was entered into between the government and the Abasand company which gave the government complete control of the operation. In fact the department takes over temporarily the assets of the Abasand company.
It is estimated that about $300,000 will be required to remodel the buildings and plant and equipment of the Abasand company. There will be drilling operations to be carried

War Appropriation-
-Mines and Resources
on as well as experimental work in the plant when it is rebuilt or revamped. Work will also have to be carried on to determine the best method of treating the bitumen when it is recovered from the sands. There is a great deal of experimental work to be done in this regard. It is definitely known now that excellent road-building material can be secured from this bitumen. It is known also that certain heavy oils can be secured, but I am informed that there is a great deal of testing work to be carried on in order that gasoline of sufficiently high quality to be of commercial value may be extracted from the sands. This work will be carried out under the agreement.
The agreement provides that within six months after the declaration of peace or the ending of a state of war the government shall have the option of buying out any equity that Abasand may still have in the plant. If there are differences of opinion provision is made that these shall be referred to the exchequer court. On the other hand, if the government does not care to exercise this option the property will be returned to the Abasand company, which will have to reimburse tlie government, not only for the moneys advanced to cover operating expense but also for any losses that have been incurred, with a rate of interest of 3J per cent on the money so advanced. I think those are the essential points of the agreement.
The next item of $500,000 would cover the revamping of the plant?
That has nothing to do with the Abasand agreement.
There is no item here that pertains to the revamping of the plant.

It was impossible to determine any definite amount, because the whole thing is really of an experimental nature. The funds required for the carrying out of the Abasand agreement will be available from the general war appropriation vote.
This vote has nothing to do with that?

Not with the Abasand
agreement.
Abasand in the agreement merely means the government. The government is operating the plant under certain gentlemen who were associated with Canadian Oils Limited.
It is entirely under the control of the government.
Is there any private capital in it at all? Is there any equity to be bought?
Oh, yes.
Who has control of that?
I have not definite knowledge as to where the capital originated on which Abasand operates.

How much private
capital is there in the Abasand company?
I do not know. They state they have spent $900,000 on development. We do not reimburse them for that.
According to the minister, if it turns out to be successful, they have a chance to recoup that $900,000 or whatever it is.
Not all of it, because part of it will be operating losses.
You do not undertake to provide anything for that?
No.

When the matter was up previously, the Minister of Munitions and Supply, speaking about the work that had been done by the Abasand company; mentioned the hydrogenation system for the extraction of the oil from the bitumen. It is quite easy to get the bitumen out, but the difficulty has been to get the oil out of the bitumen. The money that is to be spent by Abasand is not to be spent on a hydrogenation system, because that would cost a great deal of money. I am in favour of that system. If the next vote has nothing to do with that plant, I have nothing more to say at the moment.

Item agreed to.
Mines and geology branch-
Investigations of petroliferous deposits and of potential petroliferous areas in Canada, $500,000.

In the early part of the session I placed questions on the order paper with regard to oil deposits at Fort Norman and the pipeline constructed from there to White Horse. The minister asked me to take the questions off the order paper because it was not in the public interest to answer them. But within a very short time afterwards I found information in certain United States papers which answered many of the questions I had asked, especially those related to the pipeline. I believe that since then certain

4896	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
documents have been tabled in this house giving details with respect to the pipeline and the arrangements made for its return to Canada after the war. But we have never had a statement from the minister with respect to the oil deposits at Fort Norman, informing us how much money has been spent there, whether the dominion government or the Imperial Oil company is drilling wells, or what companies are interested in that field. From information we have received from other sources it is apparent that this field may develop into one of the larger oil deposits in Canada, if not on the north American continent. The minister should make a full statement on the situation, as to who is making the development and under what conditions, and how much is being spent by the government and how much by private companies.

With regard to the questions which my hon. friend put on the order paper a few months ago, as I recall it -now, we were not in a position to give the information asked for at that time as a result of an understanding with the United States authorities.
They published the information themselves within a few days.

Not a few days, but the
information was given out at Washington some time later. It was their option to give out or withhold the information.
Has Washington the authority to issue statements with respect to our own resources. It is a serious state of affairs if that is so. It seems to me that we should have the authority.
My hon. friend is getting the thing all twisted and distorted.
I have not got it twisted at all.

There was an understanding reached with the United States government concerning the Canol project, with respect to which a statement was made by the Prime Minister the other day. Certain drilling operations were carried on there for which the United States government, I understand, although I have no definite assurance on this, provided the capital. This whole development was to ensure a supply of oil for defence purposes, and since the United States government were carrying on this project we respected their wishes that publicity should not be given to it. That is why my hon. friend's question could not be answered at the time he asked it. This federal government has

not spent one dollar in development work at Fort Norman. There is not a dollar in these estimates or in the estimates of last year for that development. What we did do was to give the Imperial Oil company permits to drill for oil over a certain area. The Imperial Oil company already had leases at Fort Norman, obtained many years ago.

And had wells operating,
too.

And already had a few wells there producing oil, as well as a small refinery. There was a certain amount of fuel oil produced, and I believe some gasoline, at that refinery. I happen to know that the mining operations at Great Bear lake, where radium is produced, were carried on by means of power from diesel engines run by fuel secured from these Fort Norman wells. It was known there was oil there. The United States wished to make certain of an additional supply of oil and gasoline for war purposes and their geologists and engineers examined the territory. I do not know just what arrangements they made with Imperial Oil company. That was no particular concern of ours. We gave the Imperial Oil company some additional territory under permits. They had an area under lease there for their old development, and additional wells are being drilled. I understand that enough oil is being secured to justify the building of the pipeline. Let me repeat, that these permits were given for the purpose of finding sufficient oil to pipe to WThite Horse and from White Horse on to the defensive works in Alaska.
Will the minister table information on the areas and the concessions that have been given to the Imperial Oil company?

We have drafted a set of regulations, which have been tabled, covering the granting of permits for oil in the Northwest Territories. The permits have been issued to the company going in there to drill. We have not encouraged; we have discouraged what might be called purely speculative interests; that is, people who might think there was oil up in that country and would reserve a certain area, pay a ground rental on it for a year, and then try to sell it off to someone else who would develop it. We have discouraged that.

And given it to one
company.

We have given permits to responsible people who would go in there and develop it. There is no use in giving a permit, for instance, to some person who

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
would go in and use it for speculative purposes. After all, the government were not prepared to do the drilling there. There is not much prospect, I can assure my hon. friend, of developing oil at Fort Norman for uses other than those involved in this increased development for defence purposes, which is costing a considerable amount of money per gallon of oil when it is delivered, and for such operations as there are at Bear lake. It is not an economic proposition at the present time to develop an oil well at Fort Norman, 1,400 miles north of Edmonton. How would you get the oil to Edmonton, for instance, where it could be used? When you had got it out, transportation would cost so much that it could not for a second compete with oil from other sources. Unquestionably this development was stimulated by the state of war which existed with Japan and the need of getting oil supplies to the Alaskan frontier. That is the whole reason for this increased development. It is quite true that the government might have said, "No; because it is the Imperial Oil company we will not have anything to do with it," and we would have blocked the war effort, and that would have been that. I do not think there could be any justification for the dominion government going into an oil development 1,400 miles north of Edmonton, that might cost hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars, for uses in ordinary times.

The minister has stated that the dominion has turned over these deposits to one company to develop. None of us is quite naive enough to believe that this one company are in there for their health; that they are not getting anything out of these deposits; that they are simply developing it for war purposes without any chance of ever making anything out of it. They are certainly getting their share out of it, or they would not have developed it, and they are given a monopoly as far as this development is concerned. Whether it is economic or not depends on how much oil is there. In the United States oil is being transported great distances, from Oklahoma, near the gulf, right up to the northern states. It depends on the quantity of oil that is in the field, and if reports we hear are correct this may be a very important field. I certainly do not think the government are doing what is right in giving the company a complete monopoly of that field.

My hon. friend, of course, is quite entitled to his view; there is no doubt about that. As a matter of fact, as a purely commercial proposition you would not get 72537-3104
one oil company in ten to look at that field. I venture to say that the Imperial Oil Company have spent more money there by a long margin than they have recovered, or will recover for a good many years. That is for the simple reason that, as I stated a moment ago, it is not feasible commercially to take oil even in the quantities they have, at Fort Norman, 1,400 miles north of Edmonton, to the places where it can be used. The United States government in respect of its interest in this development asked that the permits be granted to the Imperial Oil company. Under the permits, when the war is over, we have the right to have half the area they have prospected and developed come back to the government, including half the wells and half the equipment. When my hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation come into office, as they hope to do some day, they may find this all ready for operation by then.

They will find it tied up
pretty well by one particular company. The minister's statement hardly holds water. In one breath he tells us he has to give it to one company to prevent speculators going in-

I did not say anything of
the kind.
Oh, yes, you did.

I said that the Imperial
Oil company were in there years ago; that they had developed certain works at Fort Norman, and that when this idea developed for the supply of oil and gasoline for Alaskan defence, the United States government asked that the Imperial Oil, who had had experience in the field, be given some .additional territory, and that additional territory was given under terms which I mentioned1 a moment ago, that when the war is over, the government secures, without cost one-half the development which has taken place. What my hon. friend was speaking about a moment ago, as to permits being issued, did not refer, as I understood it, to the Imperial Oil company. We could have to-day numerous speculative interests, who probably are not oil developers at all, to go in and, if we gave them a permit, preempt a certain territory in the hope that later on they could turn it over at a profit to someone who would develop it. Now we have effectively prevented that sort of thing.

Perhaps I can set the
matter straight. I mentioned the subject a short time ago. I have not any brief for the Imperial Oil, but I commend them for what they have done in that part of the country.
4898	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
They went in there quite a few years ago, and got nothing out of it commensurate with what they invested in it. They deserve credit for drilling wells at Fort Norman. I believe that" up to the time that war broke out they had had six wells more or less that perhaps could produce am average of, I understand, 300 barrels a day, at any rate not a large number. The wells did not operate for a few years, so that the company received no return outside of what oil they have sold to the radium mine on Great Bear lake and to the mines at Yellowknife on Great Slave lake. Their oil barges came up the Mackenzie river and sailed over Great Slave lake to Yellowknife and to other mining centres on Great Slave lake. Also they sent oil up the Bear- river which they had to move around the rapids of Bear river, and then on Great Bear lake to the radium mines at the east end of that lake. After the United States became embroiled in the war with Japan they wished to have oil for their war activities in Alaska. It was then they considered running a pipeline from Fort Norman over to White Horse. Other wells had been drilled by or for them, I believe, and I assume that what the minister refers to as to the United States investing in that part of the country is what they have invested in the wells they have drilled since they went there and the pipeline. From what the minister said I understand that the United States government or someone representing it has taken over for the time being the wells which were formely operated by and for the Imperial Oil company. Am I right?
No; that is not correct.

Is the Imperial Oil also
producing oil?
The United States government made an arrangement or reached an understanding with the Imperial Oil company-
That is what I said.

-to carry on drilling operations. That is according to the information that has been supplied me. What the nature of that arrangement is, how the United States government assisted the Imperial Oil company financially, or the terms upon which they assisted them, I do not know. That is a matter between the United States government and the company.
The United States government takes over all the oil produced at present at Fort Norman.
They buy oil from the operating company. The United States has not acquired title to a single oil well.

They take the oil
produced.
Yes.
I should like to obtain more information about the item. How much of this money is spent in Saskatchewan and how much in Alberta, and where is the money spent in Saskatchewan?

I understand there is only one project that is under consideration in western Saskatchewan. There is some expenditure being incurred at Wainwright in Alberta. This is to cover the investigation of petroliferous areas in Canada ; that is, possible oil areas.
Generally?
Yes.
I want to know the areas that are being investigated in Saskatchewan. How much is expended in that particular province? How much is earmarked for it?
I regret that I cannot give my hon. friend the precise location of that area. There is only one area in the southwestern part of the province.
Is no work being done in northwestern Saskatchewan in the direction of Lloydminster?
No.
Is it proposed to drill for oil at the town of Peace River or down the river from Peace River?

We have quite a number of geological parties-seventeen. We have ten parties prospecting for oil in Alberta, largely in the northern part of the province and also some over the border in British Columbia.

I was referring to the oil site at or near the town of Peace River. The minister is undoubtedly familiar with the oil formations, or evidences of oil, on the Peace river, right at the town of Peace River and down the river some twenty-five miles. Last summer I went down the river about twenty-five miles.

I cannot tell my hon. friend the precise places where these geological parties are making surveys, but I should think it likely that the area he speaks of will come under their work.

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
They are survey parties? This vote just covers survey parties?
It covers more than that.
Does it cover the actual drilling of wells in any area?
No.
Can the minister give me that information as to how much of the money is being spent or is earmarked for Saskatchewan?

There is an estimate of $10,000, but it may be more or less than that. We get a vote of $500,000. There is great urgency for oil, and consequently we have arranged for as many survey parties to go out for oil as we can get. It is impossible when you get your estimate to say just how much money you will spend here and how much you will spend there.
You have $10,000 earmarked?
Yes. Whatever is necessary for the party in Saskatchewan will be available out of this vote.
I am interested to see that enough money is available to ensure that the work is done completely in that province.
I can give my hon. friend the assurance that this party will have all the support financially that is necessary for it to carry on work throughout the summer.
Is it just one party going out in Saskatchewan?
I understand that is correct.
The minister was asked if work was being done in southwestern Saskatchewan. Are there not some leases to be worked in southeastern Saskatchewan?

No. I do not think we
have had any warrant for carrying on work there. After all, the department is guided by its trained men, its geologists, as to where the money will be spent.
Mr. FAIR. Can the minister give information with regard to the development at Wainwright?

I should have said a moment ago that work is being carried on on the seismograph principle. I hope no hon. member will ask me to explain it, because I do not know anything about it; but it is, I am informed, a scientific method of prospecting by
means that are somewhat new, and some of that seismographic work is being carried on in the Wainwright field.
Is that by dynamite and recording machines?

They drill holes in the ground and set off a blast of dynamite, and that is recorded on machines. Those who are qualified and experienced in the work can determine from the records made on the machines, or at least they can make a pretty shrewd guess, whether or not there is any oil underneath.
I believe they can find out what kind of formation it is geologically.
Probably.
How many parties does the minister propose to send out this year on this particular work?
There is a total of seventeen parties prospecting, geological parties looking for oil, and there are seven topographical parties in addition.
Are they made up of parties that are going out under the auspices of the Imperial Oil? There are parties going out drilling, sent by Imperial Oil. Is a part of this going to assist them?
Not a cent of it.
Is that all done on their own?
That is all done on their own.
I understood that a portion of this grant was being used for that purpose.
There is nothing in this vote for purposes of that kind.
Are we helping Imperial Oil? Are we paying anything towards the Imperial Oil's exploration?
No.

What
amount of assistance is given to Imperial Oil for testing the structures around the country?
We are not giving them any assistance.
None at all?
No.

What is the extent of the collaboration between the minister's depart-
4900	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
ment and the minister of natural resources of Saskatchewan? Is there any unity of purpose in the work of the minister's department and the work of that particular provincial department in connection with the explorations for which this money is being provided?

As far as the officials of
the Department of Mines and Resources are concerned, they are carrying on discussions from time to time with their opposites in the provincial field. Let me repeat that these parties are sent into certain areas on the recommendation of the experienced geologists of the department.
Of the minister's department.

Of our department. Doubtless they have obtained all the information that might be available in the provincial department; it would be their business to have all the information they could possibly get.
Does the province of Saskatchewan contribute in any way to the sort of work the minister's department is doing in this regard?
No; we bear the entire expense of the geological parties.

Do I understand that
this is the first time the federal government have resorted to the use of the seismograph in testing the oil potentialities of the various areas? I believe that for years past they have examined potential structures from a purely geological point of view, but now I understand that as a result of the present need the activities of this particular branch are being enlarged, and it is actually testing by the use of the most recent and best recognized system of seismographic test. Is that correct?

Yes; this is the first time
the seismograph has been used at federal government expense; I think I am correct in that. Our own officers do not do this work; we make agreements with experienced seismograph companies who do certain work under contract, in certain areas that we designate.

What has Doctor
Hume been using for the last several years in some of these surveys? Has he not been using this method?

He has been examining
structures, but not by seismographic methods. It may be that the seismographic methods will attain a higher state of perfection than has , been the case in the past. After all, these j methods are tried out and tested thoroughly,! and improvements made, and it may well bej

that the federal government, this government or some other government in the future, will consider it a wise expenditure to get the necessary equipment to carry on this seismographic work at government expense, but we do not have the experienced operators at this time. We recognized that there were possibilities in this method, and arrangements were made with experienced seismograph companies who, I understand, have been largely employed in the United States.
The arrangements were made with seismograph companies, does the minister say?
Yes.

Are these instruments
costly? I do not think they are very expensive, relatively, considering the use one gets out of them. In fact I think our own department has been experimenting with them for a number of years, and I find it difficult to understand-

I do not think my hon. friend is correctly informed there. I understand there are seismographic companies, principally in the United States, though no doubt they operate in other parts of the world as well, who have the instruments and trained personnel necessary for carrying on the work. At any rate our work is being carried on under an agreement with an experienced operator.
Wiiat is the agreement? Do you pay them so much per month or so much per year or so much per day?

We pay them so much a
week or so much a day; at the moment I do not know the precise terms of the agreement.

You send them to an
area and they take their equipment and carry on their investigation, and When they report they are paid for the length of time they have taken, are they not?	*

Does this item include the
cost of the investigation recently made into the shale deposits in Albert county?
That is correct.

Could the minister tell us
what was the cost of that investigation, who made it and how long it took?

We provided $50,000 for . that purpose, of which $42,611 was spent.
*0 Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury): Did the * province of New Brunswick contribute any-i thing?

Twenty-five per cent.
Was that work done under the direction of Doctor S. C. Ells?
It was under the direction of another departmental geologist.

I presume the information gained through this seismograph work is made available to the public as soon as it is obtained, and I should like the minister to tell us how that is done. I wish to know also whether there is any general policy in regard to doing seismograph work in areas already leased to development companies. I have in mind one area west of Rocky Mountain House, for instance, where there is a very large potential field. One well has been drilled there at tremendous expense, costing something over $500,000. I should assume that it would be desirable to do more intensive work in examining the potentialities of that area, but I can see also that such work would be to the benefit of a company which is already in there with a very large leasehold. The work being done by the department is desirable and commendable, but I was wondering whether the department was confining its exploratory work to areas not already leased, or whether it was giving some assistance to companies possessing areas not yet proven up.

I believe this is the first year the federal government has spent money on the seismograph method, though I understand that certain oil companies which have areas in Alberta under permit or licence have used the method, which is a common practice in the United States. However, we are not spending any money now in areas under the control of private companies. I am informed that our tests by the seismograph method will be confined almost wholly, if not entirely, to Wainwright national park, which is still under the control of the federal government. The survey may be carried outside the boundaries, but it is a new thing. The officers of the department think it has possibilities, and my judgment is that it will probably pay the government to incorporate permanently in its geological survey work the seismographic method.
Is money being spent in eastern Canada?
There have been investigations in New Brunswick, and some in Nova Scotia.
Anything in the Gaspe district?
No, nothing in the Gaspe district.
Is any work being done in the Lloydminster or Vermilion oil fields?
Some work is being done in the Vermilion district.
